articles.title: Senate Democrats pressure Schumer to cede more control over agenda
articles.summary: Democrats are using Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s (D-Md.) insurgent leadership challenge to pressure Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to give them more control over the Democratic agenda next year and to shift power away from the majority leader’s office. Democratic senators have grown tired of Schumer’s ironlike grip on the weekly discussions at the…
articles.body:
Democrats are using Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s (D-Md.) insurgent leadership challenge to pressure Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to give them more control over the Democratic agenda next year and to shift power away from the majority leader’s office.

Democratic senators have grown tired of Schumer’s ironlike grip on the weekly discussions at the Senate Democratic lunches, as well as what lawmakers describe as his obsessive control over the Democratic agenda.

The Senate Democratic caucus is filled with ambitious politicians who sometimes feels Schumer has too much control, and they want him to cede more of the spotlight if he is to return as leader.

“Everyone knows that he’s a lame duck,” said one Democratic senator who requested anonymity, predicting Schumer will not run for reelection in 2028.

Schumer hasn’t said what he will do when his Senate term expires in two years. He will turn 76 later this month.

The veteran New York senator likes to show up at almost every major Democratic press conference to help present a new proposal along with the measure’s sponsor. And sometimes he has a tough time giving up the microphone at Senate Democratic lunches, party sources say.

But even Democratic senators who are critical of Schumer’s leadership acknowledge he does some things very well.

They cite his impressive track record of raising hundreds of millions of dollars to help Democratic candidates match Republicans in television ad spending and his talent for crafting talking points to effectively counter the weekly Republican message.

At the same time, a significant number of Democratic senators feel they’re often sitting in the back seat and not playing enough of a role in making important political and policy-related decisions.

“I think that there certainly needs to be more input from the caucus — not just from the leadership — from those of us who have been here and fighting in the trenches, as well as the amazing freshmen senators” who just won their races, said Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), who hasn’t yet announced whether she’ll vote for Schumer or Van Hollen.

“I think that we need to take a look at the caucus rules and how we go about doing it,” she said. “When I served in the House, I was part of a leadership team that met with Leader Pelosi on a regular basis.”

One Schumer ally defended his outsized role as the chief spokesperson and public face of the Senate Democratic caucus by arguing he was serving as a “heat shield” for Democratic colleagues by absorbing GOP attacks when they were in the minority.

Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) said he’s trying to push his own ideas about how the Senate Democratic caucus could improve its operations and performance.

“I certainly am raising with them what I hope we could do better with the caucus to make it stronger,” said Kim, who declined to get into the details of his ideas.

The New Jersey Democrat said he has ideas on “both policy as well as just things that I think can make the caucus work stronger.”

Kim hasn’t yet declared which candidate he will support in the leadership race. The Hill is keeping a whip list of the vote count. Fourteen senators are publicly backing Schumer, compared with five in Van Hollen’s column.

Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), who’s in line to chair the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, said he wants to see committee chairs play a more active role in negotiating bills and bringing them to the floor in the next Congress.

“I think we do better work when committees are empowered. One of the things I want from leadership on both sides is to let their chairmen negotiate and get to actual good legislation. I think the more that the power is pushed down to the committee, where we have the most knowledge about how to come up with a good product, I think that benefits our ability to produce a product,” Heinrich said Tuesday morning at “The Bipartisan Blueprint: Advancing Permitting Reform for America’s Future,” an event sponsored by The Hill and JPMorgan.

Heinrich said he’s communicated his preference for giving committees more authority in the next Congress to both Schumer and Van Hollen.

“I’m making that pitch to all of the candidates,” he said.

Schumer let Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, take the lead in working with Republicans to pass the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, and he allowed Heinrich and Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), the ranking member on the Environment and Public Works Committee, to negotiate the pending bipartisan permitting reform package.

Schumer is aware of the criticisms, and one senior Democratic aide predicted, “You’re going to see less of Chuck Schumer” next year when Democrats take control of the Senate and House.

But Schumer feels confident that he’s locked up the votes to beat Van Hollen and isn’t making any public concessions.

Asked Tuesday whether he’s willing to agree to caucus reforms if reelected leader, Schumer said he’s already locked down the votes to win.

“Look, I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes. And we’re all going to roll up our sleeves and we’re going to focus on lowering costs, ending corruption. Those are the things we’re focused on.”

Schumer declined to address Van Hollen’s demand that the Democratic leader stay neutral in Democratic primaries.

Van Hollen has repeatedly hit Schumer for backing the more moderate candidates, Reps. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) and Angie Craig (D-Minn.), in the Michigan and Minnesota Senate Democratic primaries.

The winners of those contests, Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, say they’ll vote for Van Hollen as leader.

Some Democrats are ready to vote for Schumer in next month’s leadership election, but they want an indication from Schumer that he will be ready to step down from leadership at the end of this Congress, according to Democratic sources familiar with internal caucus discussions.

Former Senate Democratic Leader Harry Reid (Nev.) signaled to Senate Democratic colleagues after the 2014 midterm election, when they lost nine seats and the majority, that he would only serve one more term as leader.

Reid announced his Senate retirement in March 2015 and endorsed Schumer to succeed him as leader.

Schumer, however, hasn’t yet made any promises about limiting himself to only two more years in leadership.

Counting a 56-seat Senate majority — assuming Democrat Mary Peltola is declared victorious in Alaska — Senate Democrats feel confident they could keep control of the upper chamber through 2032, especially in light of their recent victories in deep-red states such as Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas.

Schumer appears reluctant to limit himself to only two more years in leadership when Democrats are feeling increasingly confident they could win control of the White House in the 2028 election, which would put them in position to pass landmark bills in 2029 and beyond.

articles.title: Beijing's hidden chokehold could derail Trump's $50B plan to fix America's aging skies
articles.summary: Can the United States fix its air traffic control when an expert warns China's rare earth grip could bottleneck the FAA overhaul Sean Duffy wants funded?
articles.body: Can the United States modernize its critical infrastructure without relying on China? Amid the fallout from Friday’s nationwide ground stop that halted air travel and upended plans for millions of passengers, the Trump administration blamed aging air traffic control infrastructure, pointing fingers at past administrations and calling on lawmakers to approve billions in new modernization funding. "Essentially, what you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack," President Donald Trump told reporters Monday at the White House before departing for Asia. DUFFY VOWS TO MODERNIZE AGING AIR TRAFFIC SYSTEM AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP The problem, one expert told Fox News Digital, is that China holds a near-monopoly over the global rare earth supply chain. While rare earth elements are relatively abundant in nature, Beijing dominates the processing stages required to turn raw ore into usable industrial components. "For the FAA, radars, satellite systems, complex electrical systems, precision motors, navigation systems — all of these require rare earths inside them," said Anupam Ghildyal, chief growth officer for REalloys, a North American critical minerals and rare earth company. AMERICA DEPENDS TOO MUCH ON CHINA FOR ESSENTIAL MINERALS. WE NEED TO DIG OUR FUTURE "For the FAA to upgrade the infrastructure, you need all of these components, and those components have to be manufactured here because China can limit the supply of these components to the U.S.," he added. "But to manufacture these components in the U.S., we need the basic raw materials to make them from, which is something we do not have." Beijing's stranglehold on rare earth minerals could bottleneck U.S. efforts before they get off the ground, Ghildyal warned, noting that China has the ability to slow-walk or block much-needed materials. THE WEST STILL DOESN’T GRASP THE DANGER OF CHINA’S RARE EARTH ENDGAME "100% they can, and they've been doing it," he said. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has requested $50 billion in additional funding from Congress to overhaul and modernize the nation's air traffic control system, while the White House is urging lawmakers to fund the replacement of decades-old copper wiring and aging control towers. VETERAN PILOT: CONGRESS MUST ACT TO UPDATE 'ARCHAIC' FAA TECH THAT IS 'PUTTING AMERICANS IN DANGER' "So you saw a telecom issue on Friday. We’re replacing old copper wires with fiber, but this is an old architecture of a network," Duffy said during an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity." "You’ve seen Newark go down. You’ve seen Dallas go down. You saw all of New York go down just a couple of months ago because of telecom issues. I want to build a brand-new architecture of a resilient telecom network that’s worthy of 2026 and worthy of America." China didn't always dominate the rare earth minerals trade. Many companies began outsourcing those functions overseas, which China gladly took over. GOV MIKE DUNLEAVY: CHINA IS HOLDING CRITICAL MINERALS HOSTAGE. ALASKA CAN HELP END THE THREAT "The problem is we are starting from pretty much close to zero," said Ghildyal. articles.title: Does it even matter if Alice Huang was a spy?
articles.summary: Does it really matter if Alice Huang was a spy or not?
articles.body:
It’s a tale as old as time: Boy meets girl, boy falls for girl, boy puts the entire global economy on the brink of collapse.

Well, that’s the version that’s tailor-made for our time. I am talking of course about the explosive scandal of Jensen Huang, the Taiwanese-American founder and CEO of Nvidia, the world’s second largest company, who was forced to resign over allegations that he had an affair with a Chinese spy.

The alleged spy in question is Alice Huang — a Mainland Chinese national and no relation to Jensen. She was an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that bought $2 billion worth of chips from Nvidia. Some believe she was a Chinese asset — a honeypot put in place to pass to China both Nvidia’s highly coveted chips and sensitive information about the company. For national security reasons, it is U.S. policy not to sell those chips to China.

But others have called into question the intelligence community’s assessment that Miss Huang is a spy — not least among them President Trump. “I don’t know that she is a spy,” Trump said when asked on Monday about the situation. “Usually what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy. I don’t know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don’t.”

Other allies of Jensen Huang have also cast doubt on the reporting, urging him to fight for his job and insisting no one else can do it. As of Tuesday afternoon, Jensen was asking for his old job back, posting to Twitter , “NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

But it is beside the point whether or not Alice Huang is or was a spy on the payroll of the Chinese Communist Party.

China, a totalitarian Communist regime, has no free market and no free enterprise. All entrepreneurs and executives from mainland China are by law assets of China, who operate and exist only at the party’s pleasure. They are expected — on pain of their very freedom, such as it is — to “ support, assist, and cooperate ” with China’s “national intelligence efforts.”

It is therefore irrelevant whether Alice Huang was trained in the art of spycraft or has a government pension. She was telling the Chinese Communist Party everything she could glean from her intimate affair with Jensen Huang, and smuggling chips from Megaspeed’s data centers in Malaysia to mainland China. That is what it means to be a businesswoman and a Chinese citizen.

The bigger concern was whether Jensen Huang was aware of the smuggling of Nvidia’s chips through Megaspeed (and probably a host of other companies) into China, even though the company has denied it. Huang was one of the only proponents of selling Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China — a view that predated his affair with the alleged spy.

In 2022, the Biden administration imposed strict export controls on chips to China over national security concerns, resulting in a $2 billion a year loss in sales for Nvidia. But it quickly recouped those numbers through massive sales to Singapore , which jumped from $2.3 billion in 2022 to $23.7 billion in 2024. You don’t have to be a tech genius to suspect that many of those chips were just being rerouted, then smuggled from Singapore into China.

All of this was made known to American firms, which were urged by the Commerce Department to be more careful about falling prey to smuggling schemes. Yet somehow, Nvidia took no precautions when doing business with Megaspeed, once the Singapore arm of a Chinese video game company before it turned to data center construction.

After an article in the New York Times posed questions about whether Megaspeed was smuggling Nvidia chips to China, the Times reports, Nvidia “changed how it reported geographic sales.” It erased Singapore from its financial disclosures, which, it had previously noted, “almost always shipped [products] elsewhere.”

Yet the turning of blind eyes as Nvidia were smuggled into China went even higher than Jensen Huang. A fight last week exploded between Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over this exact issue, and over why Lutnick had left Megaspeed off of a list of suspicious companies to which Nvidia is not allowed to sell chips. According to the New York Times, Lutnick repeatedly delayed or deferred controls and slowed efforts to prevent companies like Megaspeed from accessing Nvidia chips. Related fact: Cantor Fitzgerald, Lutnick’s investment firm (now run by his sons), is deeply invested in Nvidia and is itself financing the construction of data centers in Malaysia.

And it must be asked: Was Lutnick fulfilling the wishes of Trump himself, who is close with Jensen Huang and has a green-light approach to AI in general?

Does it really matter if Alice Huang was a spy or not, if even the Trump administration was shrugging at the sale of Nvidia chips to companies that were strongly suspected of smuggling them into China?

On Monday, the Trump administration announced it would impose a new rule to clamp down on the loophole that allowed China to access Nvidia chips through companies like Megaspeed. The new rule requires overseas data centers to get a government license before selling “significant volumes of computing power” to companies with headquarters in high-risk countries like China.

Good. But the new rule coming so soon on the heels of scandal looks like a tacit admission of guilt — and of how high up the problem went.

Batya Ungar Sargon is the host of “ Batya !” which airs Saturday nights at 7 p.m. Eastern Time on NewsNation, the fastest-growing cable news network in the U.S. and a sister company of The Hill.

articles.title: Tech outages spark mounting questions
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Peltola win completes blue wave ▪ Nvidia board rejects Huang comeback ▪ Jeffries expected to win leadership vote ▪ Dirty bomb report sparks fears Figures across the political spectrum are demanding an explanation for the series of technology outages affecting various industries over the past week, including the highly unusual Federal…
articles.body:
▪ Jeffries expected to win leadership vote

Figures across the political spectrum are demanding an explanation for the series of technology outages affecting various industries over the past week, including the highly unusual Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop on Friday.

“Americans aren’t stupid. We want and deserve to know what’s really going on,” Tricia McLaughlin , a former spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, said in a post on the social platform X.

Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) in a social media post called on the administration to immediately brief Congress on the “exact nature” of the problem to ensure an “all of government response.”

“While some of this may be coincidental, it is clear we must take cybersecurity and the nefarious use of AI seriously — and act without delay,” he said.

The outages continued to pile up on Tuesday.

The classified network used for the National Security Agency’s (NSA) internal communications experienced what the agency called a “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance. The NSA said some internal systems were affected, but “mission-critical capabilities” remain operational.

Users reported a wide range of issues with Apple services and products , including iCloud, Apple Pay, the App store and AppleCare. The company said it identified a “security incident” in which an “unauthorized party” exploited a vulnerability and used it to add malicious JavaScript programming to some projects.

The day before, malicious JavaScript was apparently used to target visitors to websites belonging to 178 organizations, including some of the most-visited ones worldwide, like Zoom, CNN, Salesforce and Ikea.

The code was intended to infect iPhones and steal cryptocurrency by capturing payment card details, stealing cookies and other measures. The code targeted the websites through the website optimization platform Optimizely, which said the vulnerability was fixed.

Also on Monday, customers at five major banks reported trouble accessing their accounts, apparently because of a software issue.

Before the FAA outage last week, Microsoft’s Outlook email system crashed for millions of users worldwide.

President Trump largely brushed off the recent string of outages, saying, “It’s life.”

“When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen,” he said in Manila, Philippines, on Tuesday.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Secretary of State Marco Rubio tried to offer more reassuring messages later in the day.

“Let me tell you what this is not, as far as we can tell … this is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state. We’ve looked very closely,” Clayton told CNBC as markets were rattled by the outages.

Clayton said that tech infrastructure “upgrades” — including the integration of AI — may have led to the recent issues.

“We are not under systemic attack,” Rubio told reporters in Manila, Philippines.

“Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cyber-criminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country,” he added.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he spoke to a tech expert who also believed artificial intelligence, which the administration calls super intelligence (SI), could be responsible .

“When they put in a program that’s able to write codes and it goes in, it self-fixes itself,” he said during an interview on Fox News. “It’s like doing a change order on a house. When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing, that’s a ripple effect. And it causes a system to be overran that weren’t designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy gave a briefing to Senate Republicans during their luncheon Tuesday, leaving Democrats out.

Following the briefing, he told reporters that officials still don’t have “clarity” on what caused the FAA issue, but the investigation is ongoing. Officials have said the issue stemmed from an overload of data on routers.

Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.), the vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said in a statement that there is “no indication” that the incidents are a result of a cyberattack, foreign interference or a coordinated effort. He said they seem to be a result of how AI is quickly changing cybersecurity, adding that the disruptions should be a “wake-up call.”

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) called for a briefing for the full Senate.

“I mean, if that is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world,” he said. “You can’t tell me that all of this is just happenstance. So, I’m completely in the dark, and people at home are in the dark, and they shouldn’t be. So we should get answers.”

▪ The Hill Insider : Duffy’s air traffic control push hits bipartisan resistance.

▪ The Hill : Hakeem Jeffries demands high-level briefing on outages.

TUNE IN : Coming off the uncertainty concerning the aviation industry, join The Hill in partnership with Airlines for America today for “Red, Flight & Blue: The Future of U.S. Aviation.” We bring together industry leaders, lawmakers, and stakeholders for a discussion on this critical moment in aviation as the industry gears up for one of the busiest seasons of the year.

The White House has pulled the nomination of Heidi Overton to serve as the head of the Food and Drug Administration, just ahead of her scheduled confirmation vote before the Senate health committee. The administration cited opposition from Senate Republicans, but the committee’s chair, Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), said she had a “viable confirmation path.”

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the U.S. would “work to regain” its measles elimination status after officially losing it Tuesday amid a sharp rise in cases. Democrats have largely blamed Trump and Kennedy for contributing to the development through adding doubts about vaccines and the scientific community.

Trump has formally nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to be the Army’s new chief of staff , months after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired his predecessor. LaNeve has served in the acting role for months. His nomination is likely to face pushback from members of both parties.

Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks at an election night event Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Anchorage, Alaska. (AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson)

THE LAST FRONTIER : Democrat Mary Peltola has officially flipped Alaska’s Senate seat in her race against Sen. Dan Sullivan (R), completing the historic blue wave of the midterms in the upper chamber.

Peltola’s victory seemed increasingly likely over the past week as she expanded her lead. The most recent vote drop last night moved her total support to above 50 percent, leading to Decision Desk HQ’s projection . That sets her on track to avoid needing Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation to win.

The win brings Democrats’ total number of flips in the Senate to nine, cementing a 56-44 majority in the next session of Congress. While the party had been strongly favored heading into Election Day, that’s still a stunning turnaround from its widespread defeats in the 2024 cycle, particularly given the uphill battle it was facing in states that voted for Trump by double digits.

With her election, Peltola will become the first Alaska Native to serve in the Senate and one of the first two Native American women senators, along with Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.).

▪ The Hill : Why an Alaska win by Peltola is so important to Democrats.

▪ The Hill : Lisa Murkowski calls midterms a ‘direct pushback’ to Trump.

DON’T CALL IT A COMEBACK : Nvidia’s board has rejected former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ‘s offer to return as the head of the company in the aftermath of his resignation over his multiple affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.

Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of the company’s quarterly earnings call that the board unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and doesn’t intend to reinstate him .

Huang broke his silence Tuesday for the first time since resigning from the company last week, expressing his willingness to return should the board allow it.

Huang nodded to the mounting calls for his return, including from tech billionaire Elon Musk , writing in a statement, “Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company.”

Trump said Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang was reinstated as CEO.

Multiple lawmakers also announced yesterday that Huang has agreed to appear before multiple panels for testimony.

▪ The Hill : Nvidia reports strong third quarter after Huang departs.

▪ The Hill : Democratic lawmakers slam Huang statement on possible Nvidia return.

LEADERSHIP VOTE: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is expected to be nominated as Speaker when House Democrats meet this morning to elect their leadership team.

No other Democrat has thrown their hat in the ring to be considered for the position, but The Hill’s Mike Lillis and Sudiksha Kochi report that the path to the Speakership won’t be a cakewalk either. There have been rumblings about leadership change from left-leaning groups as well as the incoming crop of first-year lawmakers, who will not participate in today’s vote but who will take part in the formal full House S peaker vote on Jan. 3.

Jeffries has a cushion of roughly 40 votes to still reach the necessary 218-vote threshold in January, thanks to sweeping Democratic election victories.

Multiple reports have indicated that Jeffries plans to push members to take a tallied vote on his nomination today, which could give him a sense of whether he has enough votes before the full House votes at the start of next year.

▪ The Hill : Chuck Schumer says he has the votes to be elected majority leader.

▪ The Hill : Lawmakers stress urgency on permitting reform bill.

The president is in Shenzhen, China. He will participate in an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ family photo at 8:30 p.m. EST and an APEC plenary session at 8:45 p.m. EST. He will participate in a bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at 11:45 p.m. EST.

The House and Senate will convene at 10 a.m.

A woman holds an Iranian flag as part of a pro-government campaign in downtown Tehran, Iran, Monday, Nov. 16, 2026. (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi)

DIRTY BOMB PLOT: Reports that Iran has planned an alleged “dirty bomb” attack in Washington, D.C., is causing a stir in the nation’s capital and raising new questions about the potential targets, the danger of the reported weapon and whether Iran even has the capability of carrying out such an attack.

U.S. intelligence reportedly picked up claims from Iran that it has stashed material in the United States to build a dirty bomb, which spreads radioactive contamination and is seen as particularly harmful in dense urban environments. A dirty bomb is also considered relatively easy to assemble and does not necessarily require someone to enter the country to detonate, leaving the U.S. particularly vulnerable to such attacks.

CNN reported that the intelligence indicates Tehran is developing plans to target senior officials in the Trump administration with the chemical weapons. Another line of intelligence, The New York Times first reported, suggests Iran could deploy chemical weapons against U.S. service members, as well as diplomatic and intelligence personnel stationed in the Middle East.

Sources familiar with the latest intelligence tell CNN, however, that the planning is currently seen as the Iranian regime giving itself options as the war stretches on and not an indication of an imminent attack.

The White House said in a statement the U.S. is “ monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.” The president was also asked about the reports and said officials were taking the threat seriously and cautioned that Iran would “pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before” if it attacked Washington.

Iran has adamantly denied the allegations, with a foreign ministry spokesperson calling the report “baseless” and a “fabricated media narrative.”

Residents take to the streets to demonstrate their support for Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele and the deployment of Salvadoran soldiers to fight armed gangs in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (AP Photo/Patrice Noel)

NEW CHAPTER : Haiti is gearing up for its first presidential election in more than a decade, if the chaos that has troubled the country for years doesn’t result in more delays.

The registration window for candidates has now closed, and more than 30 candidates filed to run for the office. The country’s electoral council is reviewing the filings and expects to produce a finalized list of names cleared to run in January. Some high-profile names are among the candidates, including three women for the first time in Haiti’s history.

The Caribbean nation hasn’t had a president since Jovenal Moïse was assassinated in 2021 as part of a failed attempt to take over the government. One of the candidates is Moïse’s widow, former Haitian first lady Martine Moïse . Former acting Prime Minister Claude Joseph is also seeking the role.

Both Martine Moïse and Joseph were indicted following Jovenal Moïse’s assassination tied to his death, but the charges were dropped last year.

Other notable candidates include former President Michel Martelly , economist Etzer Emile and former foreign affairs minister Dominique Dupuy .

Haiti has been led by appointed prime ministers and a presidential transition council since Jovenal Moïse’s death. The country plans to hold a first round of voting in July and a second round in October, but some experts remain skeptical that Haiti will be ready for these elections.

Gang violence still dominates in much of the country, with militias fighting against Haitian soldiers and police and a U.N.-backed gang suppression force. And the number of clashes and fatalities have been ticking up recently.

Hakeem Jeffries’s road to the Speakership will be nothing like Nancy Pelosi’s in 2018 , former Rep. Steve Israel (D-N.Y.) writes in The Hill.

Americans don’t care about beating China’s AI; we’d rather have safety , Michael Fuchs writes in The Hill.

And finally … Pope Leo XIV said he forgave the person who threw a rosary at him that hit him in the eye during his recent trip to Peru.

Leo just concluded a 12-day trip to South America following his successful cancer surgery. Worshippers often toss certain items at the pope, such as rosaries, stuffed animals and papal dolls, The Washington Post reported .

Leo joked as he headed back to Rome that the thrown rosary was a sign of the person’s “faith.”

“The dearness of the Peruvians, including the person with a lot of faith who simply wanted to offer me a rosary, may be the things that you carry in your heart — or maybe the eye — that mark the life of someone,” he said.

articles.title: Asylum is a privilege — treat it like one
articles.summary: Congress needs to reform the system — an executive proclamation probably isn’t enough.
articles.body:
The Supreme Court agreed last week to hear Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services , the case surrounding President Trump’s proclamation of a border “invasion.” Before the briefs pile up, let’s settle what both camps keep skipping: Asylum is a privilege that Congress grants, and Congress can attach conditions to it.

Trump’s proclamation declared the southern border under invasion and shut the asylum door to those crossing it. A three-judge panel on the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled two to one against the administration in April, holding that presidents may suspend entry but may not override the procedures established by Congress.

I read that ruling the way I read a commercial lease: slowly, hunting for the trap. The panel has a point.

The late Justice Antonin Scalia insisted that “the text is the law, and it is the text that must be observed.” Conservatives love that line until it bumps into our own side. Federal law lets any alien physically present in the U.S. apply for asylum “irrespective of such alien’s status.” That’s a right to apply. The grant, however, is a different animal, because the law states that the government “may grant” asylum, not that it must. Since the 1987 case INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca in 1987, the court has treated asylum as discretionary and withholding of removal as mandatory. So the grant is a privilege, and the application is a statutory right. A proclamation cannot erase one by renaming the other.

This Supreme Court will read the statute for the executive when the text allows it. In June, it ruled 6-3 in Mullin v. Al Otro Lado that a migrant standing in Mexico has not arrived in the United States.

Congress also drew the privilege narrowly. The definition requires persecution, or a well-founded fear of it, on account of race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership in a particular social group. Poverty, however real or dire it is, is not grounds for asylum.

The front door matters too. Under expedited removal , an immigrant who tells an officer he fears persecution gets a credible fear interview instead of a quick removal. But in a system as clogged as ours, that reasonable first look can stretch into years.

Now the practical problem: TRAC reports that there were over 3 million active cases in immigration court at the end of September, including 2.3 million waiting on asylum hearings. The backlog has become the Hotel California of the legal system, where anyone can check in and nobody checks out. A statute of limitations exists because cases left open forever reward whoever runs out the clock. A claim filed today buys years in the U.S., whether it’s strong or weak. Delay is the incentive.

Fraud feeds on that delay. In 2022, federal prosecutors in Manhattan convicted a Brooklyn immigration-services executive and an attorney of conspiring to commit immigration fraud, in a scheme that coached clients before their sworn interviews with asylum officers. Every invented persecution story pushes a genuine one further back in line. Honest refugees are the first victims of the cheats, which is why the compassionate position is to detect and deport the cheats as quickly as possible.

Congress needs to reform this system, because no executive can do so alone. First, asylum applicants should be required to swear an oath to “absolutely and entirely renounce and abjure all allegiance” the moment they are granted asylum. You might think that’s performative — I prefer to have it on the record.

Grantees should also be required to go ten years with no federal means-tested benefits. Congress has already cut SNAP for refugees and asylees in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, leaving green card holders as the main exception. This extends the same principle.

Critics will call this cruel and quote the poem on the base of the Statue of Liberty. I would answer that a person fleeing death squads doesn’t need food stamps to justify the trip. Edmund Burke described society as a partnership that reaches the dead and “those who are to be born,” and partners read the terms before they sign. A genuine refugee accepts those terms gladly. To add conditions is to screen for the people the statute was actually written for.

I raised three sons on a simple rule: ask for help when you need it, but plan to carry your own weight. An immigration policy built on the same rule would survive more than one administration.

The justices in this case need to decide whether a proclamation can do what only a statute should. Congress should stop outsourcing the hard part. A country that can’t tell a true refugee from a freeloader ends up failing both. Write the terms, pass them, and let the lifeboat do its work.

Jay Rogers is a financial professional with more than 30 years of experience in private equity, private credit, hedge funds, and wealth management.

articles.title: Trump’s grip on GOP faces major post-election test as his hand-picked leader faces challenge from within
articles.summary: President Donald Trump is working to save RNC Chair Joe Gruters from a re-election challenge by co-Chair KC Crosbie after GOP midterm election losses.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's handpicked leader of the Republican National Committee (RNC) is facing a challenge from within his own leadership team after Republicans suffered sweeping losses in the midterm elections that saw even historically deep red seats flip blue in states like Texas, Mississippi and South Carolina. RNC Chair Joe Gruters, who is seeking a full two-year term running the national party committee, will face-off with co-Chair KC Crosbie of Kentucky after Democrats captured sizable majorities in both the House and Senate and prepare to retake control in January. Crosbie, a staunch Trump supporter, launched her bid just days after the elections, seeking to capitalize on frustration among Republicans over the party's losses and build support for a change in leadership. "I hope to speak with each of you before then. I want to hear what you saw in your states, what you think we need to change, and how we can put our Party in a stronger position for the next election," Crosbie wrote in a letter to the 168 RNC committee members, who will vote for the next chair when the party holds its winter meeting in Arizona in mid-January. FIRST ON FOX: PENCE LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO 2028 WHITE HOUSE RUN Some party insiders tell Fox News that Gruters is expected to win re-election, thanks to support from President Trump — but others familiar with the mood of the RNC membership said support for Crosbie is growing. Trump, who installed Gruters as party chair 15 months ago after he urged then-Chair Michael Whatley to run for the Senate in North Carolina, quickly endorsed him in the days after the midterms to earn a full term at the helm. "Joe Gruters should return as Chairman of the RNC to continue to build our Party, and be a trusted partner as we MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN, and ensure Free and Fair Elections," Trump wrote on social media. A source confirmed to Fox News Digital that the president has been working behind the scenes to shore up support for Gruters and also confirmed an Axios report that the president threatened retribution against the RNC if the chair isn't re-elected. WILL TRUMP AVOID MAKING AN ENDORSEMENT IN THE 2028 GOP NOMINATION RACE? An aide in Gruters' political orbit told Fox News Digital that the chairman is hitting the phones and reaching out to committee members — and the calls are going well. They highlighted how the RNC had historic fundraising over the past year under Gruters' leadership and that he made over 40 campaign stops in 14 states during the midterm election's final stretch while working directly with members and state party chairs on a daily basis. Fox News Digital has also confirmed an AP report regarding Gruters' letter to RNC members last week, when he defended specific expenditures that have raised concerns among the party membership. Nevada GOP Chair Michael McDonald told Fox News Digital that "it comes down to this. President Trump has made his choice. He's the leader of our party. This is who they want to go with, and we have to get behind our leaders and regroup." McDonald praised Gruters for his "personal touch" and said, "KC's a dear friend, so I don't have anything bad to say about her." But he added, "We have to focus on looking out and not looking in and having internal fights. So I hope everybody comes together on this and gets behind Joe ... we have to move this party forward behind what the president wants." Longtime Iowa GOP chair Jeff Kaufmann praised Gruters for sending "some of the best RNC staffers and directors on the ground out here that I could ever hope for. The resources given to us were amazing." And Kaufmann emphasized, "President Trump has unambiguously and very strongly endorsed Joe Gruters and that’s all I need." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER In the wake of the ballot box setbacks, no party-led autopsy appears to be in the works. And Crosbie, in her letter to committee members, pointed to the midterms and emphasized "we lost races in places we have long counted on. We owe ourselves an honest account of why." "Voters were focused on the cost of living and the direction of the country. Our improvements in field operations, voter contact, and election-integrity infrastructure were valuable, but they did not answer those concerns or deliver the results we needed," she emphasized. "Some voters who supported us in 2024 stayed home or voted differently in 2026. We must ask whether we addressed the issues that mattered most to them, gave our candidates the support they needed, and nominated candidates who could win the races before them." RNC member Oscar Brock of Tennessee, who is supporting Crosbie’s candidacy, told Fox News Digital "the goal of the national party is to elect Republicans and that’s true across the country." "While we have traditionally deferred to the president to suggest who should be the national committee chairman, in this case we would hope the president would change his mind, because those of us who are supporting KC Crosbie for national chairman see Joe as having failed to do a successful job," Brock said. Sue Cienki, an RNC committee member from Rhode Island, said KC is a member's member. She's done a great outreach the past couple of years" and added, "I don't think the members know Joe as well as they know KC. We had a devastating loss on Election Day and I think people are looking for some sort of change," Cienki added. "It's not, in any way, shape or form, an insult to the president. I think that we're all in the 168 supportive of his policies, and we want to make sure the next two years go as smoothly for him as possible. But we are a separate entity from the White House." But Gruters supporters highlighted his fundraising and organizational efforts. RNC committee member from Maine Lauren LePage told Fox News Gruters was "incredibly responsive this cycle...he’s raised a ton of money for the party and supported candidates up and down the ballot ... although we suffered some losses, Chairman Gruters certainly did his job." LePage, whose father, former two-term Maine Gov. Paul LePage, captured a Democrat-controlled open congressional seat in a rare midterm flip for the GOP, said that the RNC "made enormous investments in the ground game in Maine that resulted in a victory in CD 2." In neighboring New Hampshire, RNC committee member Bill O'Brien pointed to Gruters and Crosbie and said, "I think there are two good candidates. I like them both." But O'Brien, a former state House speaker, said, "2028 starts now, and Joe Gruters is the leader we need at the RNC to win." "We need to build our war chest, strengthen our state parties, and protect the ballot. I’m proud to support Joe’s reelection as RNC chairman," O'Brien added. "We need proven leadership so we can fire on all cylinders and stay in the fight." Another RNC committee member, who asked to remain anonymous to speak more freely, said "I’m with Joe. Nobody’s happy with the election, but it’s nothing against Joe. It’s nothing Joe could control." "When your party has the White House, with all due respect to the chair, the RNC is an arm of the White House and so if people have a beef or a grievance, it’s with the White House, not with Joe. And so I think it would be unfair to hold Joe accountable," the committee member emphasized. Since Trump's first election to the White House a decade ago, the RNC has experienced significant membership turnover, with those coming on board seen as loyal supporters of the president. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Former longtime RNC committee member from Mississippi Henry Barbour, who left the committee two years ago after serving for nearly two decades, told Fox News Digital, "Historically, anytime the White House has a candidate for RNC chair, they win, and I expect that Gruters will win." "But I do think we need to have a discussion about the future of the party and what’s at stake and how do we get back on a winning path," Barbour added. "The only job of a political party is to win elections. That’s the number one job, and we’re failing at it."

articles.title: Why lame-duck Republicans are blocking Trump’s judicial picks
articles.summary: Watch The Gavel Live: Hill Insider members can join us live today at 3 p.m. EST as we discuss the vibes at the Federalist Society’s convention, the biggest gathering of the year for the conservative legal movement, in the wake of Democrats’ midterm sweep. Senate Republicans are hitting some surprising hurdles as they race to confirm as…
articles.body:
Watch The Gavel Live: Hill Insider members can join us live today at 3 p.m. EST as we discuss the vibes at the Federalist Society’s convention, the biggest gathering of the year for the conservative legal movement, in the wake of Democrats’ midterm sweep.

Senate Republicans are hitting some surprising hurdles as they race to confirm as many of President Trump’s judicial picks as possible in the 46 days they have before Democrats take control of Congress.

Arkansas’s senators successfully blocked one of Trump’s circuit court nominees.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) doesn’t seem to care for the president nominating a Justice Department official to a judgeship in his state.

And Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) is signaling there will be a battle to confirm an Oklahoma nominee.

The Senate Judiciary Committee under Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) is moving quickly despite the problems.

Grassley scheduled back-to-back hearings this week in an effort to advance nominees, a “mad scramble” that Democrats argue violates longstanding norms.

“Remember this day when a future Democratic chair moves judicial nominees through the committee with one week for you to review their background and qualifications for a lifetime appointment,” Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois), the committee’s ranking member, warned his Republican colleagues on Tuesday.

Many of the battles are being waged by lame-duck Republican senators whose relationships with Trump have frayed.

Cornyn has become a thorn in Trump’s side in his final months as a senator, showing an increased willingness to use his leverage to hold up legislation and appointments he opposes. It’s made some GOP observers unhappy.

“Politics, more often than it should be, is high school,” Mike Fragoso , who previously advised Sen. Mitch McConnell’ s (R-Ky.) and Grassley, wrote on social media .

“Does it have to be? That’s the question left to individual politicians, like John Cornyn, who—in the end—are accountable only for themselves and their own choices,” Fragoso continued.

Cornyn, who will exit the Senate at the end of this Congress, has refused to submit a blue slip for T. Elliot Gaiser , the head of the DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel, effectively blocking his confirmation hearing for a seat on the U.S. District Court in the Northern District of Texas.

Refresh: The “blue slip” process is a tradition in which the Senate Judiciary Committee chairman asks home-state senators to assess the nomination of a U.S. district court nominee. If the form is withheld or returned with objections, the nomination typically does not move forward.

A Cornyn aide tells The Gavel he has instead been pushing the White House for months to recommend Steve Fahey , a former federal prosecutor, for the vacancy.

“The purpose of advice and consent is to have a consultation, and the White House has completely ignored that,” Cornyn told reporters in the Capitol on Monday. “And I don’t want the seat to go vacant, so we’ve recommended somebody who can be confirmed. But I’m not willing to let the White House ignore the Senate’s constitutional role.”

In Arkansas, Republican Sens. Tom Cotton and John Boozman successfully tanked Trump’s nominee to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8 th Circuit, Lee Rudofsky , to the chagrin of some conservatives.

Their pressure led to Trump to swap out Rudofsky for the duo’s pick, Arkansas Supreme Court Justice Cody Hiland.

It was a nod that Hiland expected to get — only months earlier. He told a room full of law students at the University of Arkansas in August that he had already gone through the vetting process for the 8 th Circuit job when the White House changed course and offered him a district court seat instead.

He turned it down, recounting the surprised reaction he received from White House counsel on the other end of the phone call.

“He said, ‘So you want me to go back into the Oval Office and tell the President of the United States that you’re rejecting an opportunity to be appointed to the federal bench, and I said, ‘Yes, that’s exactly what I want you to tell the president of the United States,'” Hiland recalled .

A battle is also emerging in Oklahoma over Trump’s selection of Zach West and Trevor Pemberton to federal judgeships in the state.

Both nominations were on the Judiciary Committee’s agenda Tuesday, but their names were skipped over without explanation. Like the Arkansas standoff, some conservative lawyers have their eyes laser-focused on the clock.

“I have it on very good authority that Oklahomans will either have two new judges soon or they will have zero new judges for at least two years,” Rob Luther , who previously worked in the White House counsel’s office under Trump, wrote on social media two days before the hearing.

Luther’s assessment followed an earlier Reuters report that indicated Sen. Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.) had pulled back his support for West after previously returning a blue slip. That position has Tillis’ backing, according to the outlet, which complicates the confirmation math as Republicans can afford only one defection on party-line votes.

It’s not over yet. Kevin Hern , who won the election in November to permanently fill the Senate seat currently held by Armstrong, is set to be sworn in at the end of the month. He told Bloomberg he’ll support Trump’s pick, and Tillis signaled he may also be willing to drop his opposition.

“Frankly, it’s an unforced error by the White House just not to consult more effectively with Senator Armstrong,” Tillis reportedly said. “I think he’ll get done, but they’re running it down to the wire.”

Welcome to The Gavel, The Hill’s weekly newsletter unpacking the intersection of courts & politics from Zach Schonfeld and Sophie Brams. Email us tips at zschonfeld@thehill.com and sbrams@thehill.com . You can also reach out to us on X (@ZachASchonfeld and @sophiebrams) or Signal (zachschonfeld.48 and sbrams.32).

Lucas targets top admin officials: Virginia Senate President Pro Tem L. Louise Lucas (D) is asking a federal judge to sanction Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel for “extrajudicial statements” made during a public press conference in October announcing charges related to an alleged marijuana conspiracy scheme.

Trump’s East Potomac plans hit snag : East Potomac Park remains open to the public after U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes blocked the Trump administration from closing it for at least two weeks, a setback for Trump in his bid to redevelop the golf courses into a single championship-level facility capable of hosting major professional tournaments.

Dems, DOJ trade threats ahead of oversight blitz: Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, is firing warning shots at incoming House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) and other senators as Democrats prepare to launch an investigative blitz into the Trump administration’s activities when they return to power.

Conservative justices in FedSoc spotlight : Justices Amy Coney Barrett, Neil Gorsuch and Brett Kavanaugh reflected on the nation’s 250 th anniversary in a series of pre-taped interviews for the Federalist Society’s annual National Lawyers Conference last week. Justice Samuel Alito delivered a surprise speech during the Antonin Scalia Memorial Dinner, warning that the Supreme Court was “vulnerable” to Congress and the executive branch.

Clancy gets retrial date: Lindsey Clancy will go back on trial in early March for the alleged murders of her three young children in 2023, a Massachusetts judge has decided. The state’s first attempt to prosecute Clancy ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she should be held criminally liable for the deaths.

Federalist Society convention attendees were invited to sit down for lunch with conservative federal judges and learn about their hobbies. We took notes. Here are some of our favorites (join us on the live show for the full listing)

Emil Bove , 3 rd Circuit: “Off-Grid Living”

James Ho , 5 th Circuit: “You’ve Got to Have Hobbies”

Rebecca Taibleson , 7 th Circuit: “True Crime Media”

Patrick Bumatay , 9 th Circuit: “Horror Movies”

“The Best Justice System in the World,” a new documentary by University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign law professor Suja Thomas that explores the flaws of the U.S. justice system, premiered at the DOC NYC Film Festival over the weekend. Watch the trailer .

Harvard Law School has postponed the remaining qualifying and semifinal rounds of its prestigious Ames Moot Court Competition until next spring due to an ongoing strike by the Harvard Graduate Students Union-United Auto Workers. Read more from The Harvard Law Record.

A wrinkle in the Supreme Court battle over AR-15s

A major gun battle is headed to the justices next month. Or is it?

Weeks ahead of oral arguments on whether states can ban AR-15s and semiautomatic rifles, one of the plaintiffs is dropping out of the case.

Cutberto Viramontes provided no explanation for his decision, which throws a potential wrinkle into the blockbuster Second Amendment battle set to impact bans in nearly a dozen blue states.

Everyone had agreed Viramontes had legal standing to bring the challenge. He wanted to buy an AR-15, and Cook County, Ill. — which includes Chicago — prevents him from doing so.

The other individual suing alongside him, Christopher Khaya , wants to own an IMI Galil semiautomatic rifle.

And that’s relevant, the county says, because the Supreme Court took up the case only to decide if the Second Amendment protects “AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles.” Cook County says Khaya’s desired firearm is more like an AK-47, not an AR-15, so he isn’t a suitable challenger.

“Should petitioners disavow their prior statement and argue that the IMI Galil weapon is ‘similar’ to an AR-15, the record would not support that about-face. There are no record facts concerning whether the IMI Galil weapon operates similarly to an AR-15,” Cook County wrote to the justices .

The county wants the Supreme Court to throw out the lawsuit.

The challengers’ lawyers say the Supreme Court should proceed as normal, arguing that Khaya and the gun rights groups suing, the Firearms Policy Coalition and the Second Amendment Foundation, all have standing.

“Indeed, until now, the County’s litigation position has been that the rifles are interchangeable,” they wrote in court filings .

The Supreme Court has yet to resolve the dispute as the oral arguments approach.

Whichever way it shakes out, don’t expect the AR-15 battle to completely fizzle out at the Supreme Court.

Alongside the Chicago-area lawsuit, they’ve taken up a challenge to a similar law in Connecticut. No one has suggested a standing problem there.

Cases the Supreme Court is taking up — or passing on — this term.

The Supreme Court turned away dozens of cases at its final meeting of the November session, but it took up two new ones. We highlighted both in last week’s edition as ones to keep an eye on:

In Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, the justices will decide if President Trump’s asylum ban is legal.

On Inauguration Day, Trump declared an invasion at the southern border to effectively shut down asylum applications. Lower courts ruled it exceeded his authority, though they have allowed the ban to remain in place as the case proceeds.

It sets the stage for another massive Supreme Court showdown over Trump’s immigration crackdown. The justices are also mulling if Trump can deport migrants to countries where they have no ties and if authorities can indefinitely detain migrants without giving them access to a bond hearing.

The second case is Robinhood Markets v. Sodha , an investor lawsuit against the fintech company claiming it omitted key details about its business during its public offering amid the meme stock craze. The justices will sort out the standards for lawsuits under Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, and whether the accusations against Robinhood can proceed.

In a rather unusual move, the court rebuffed the Trump administration’s ask to take up its appeal in another hot-button legal battle, Trump v. Thakur.

A lower court has blocked the administration from cutting off grants to University of California researchers in response to Trump’s executive orders that seek to eliminate diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies.

The Supreme Court turned away Solicitor General D. John Sauer ’s ask to review the decision. Though the denial is far from unprecedented, the court often agrees to requests from the sitting administration.

The court provided no explanation for its decision, and no justice publicly dissented.

Separately, we have an update on two other petitions we told you to watch. The court won’t be taking them up, but a justice was writing an opinion behind the scenes. They dropped Monday:

Dive deeper here on why three conservative justices wanted to hear a free-speech challenge to California’s requirement that instructors teach doctors renewing their medical licenses about implicit bias.

And dive deeper here into the court’s decision to turn away a challenge to a Maryland gun law, and what Justice Clarence Thomas is signaling to Second Amendment advocates.

A federal judge in D.C. will hold a status conference in the criminal case against Rahmanullah Lakanwal , who is accused of shooting of two National Guard members who were on duty in the nation’s capital last year. Lakanwal has experienced several health-related setbacks while in jail, requiring him to be forcibly fed by prison officials.

Jeanine John Taele, who was arrested at Trump National Golf Club in Rancho Palos Verdes days before a planned visit by the president in early August, is set to appear in a Los Angeles courtroom for a hearing on whether he is mentally competent to stand trial on state weapons charges.

Influencer Andrew Tate will appear in a Miami courtroom for a hearing as he fights extradition to the United Kingdom on rape, assault, trafficking for sexual exploitation and other related charges.

A federal judge in New York will hold a hearing as Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, one of three men accused of plotting nearly 20 terror attacks targeting U.S. citizens and Jewish communities in Europe, potentially seeks to represent himself in court.

A federal judge in D.C. will hear arguments as the Trump administration seeks to dissolve a preliminary injunction blocking the renaming and closure of the Kennedy Center.

Influencer Tristan Tate will appear in a Miami courtroom for a hearing as he fights extradition to the United Kingdom on rape, assault, trafficking for sexual exploitation and other related charges.

A federal judge in D.C. will hold a hearing to discuss pre-trial discovery in the case against Elias Rodriguez , the suspect charged in the fatal May 2025 shooting of two Israeli Embassy staffers outside the Capital Jewish Museum.

A federal judge in D.C. will hear arguments in a lawsuit filed by Arlington County, Va., that seeks to block construction of a 250-foot triumphal arch. The project has already been temporarily stopped in a separate case.

A federal judge in D.C. will hold a virtual status conference for updates in The American Federation of Teachers’ lawsuit against the Education Department for shutting down access to income-driven repayment plans for student borrowers.

A federal judge in D.C. will hear arguments in a lawsuit challenging the Education Department’s cuts to the Institute of Education Sciences which the Trump administration wants dismissed.

Trump wrote in a Truth Social post that he had a “wonderful meeting on Trade, National Security, and other subjects” with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. “I am…
articles.body:
President Trump said Wednesday that the United States made a “landmark” trade deal with the Philippines that would great for American famers, but offered no further details.

Trump wrote in a Truth Social post that he had a “wonderful meeting on Trade, National Security, and other subjects” with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

“I am pleased to announce that we made a new and completely different Trade Deal with the Philippines, one that will be a true landmark and, in particular, a Deal that will be great for our Farmers and those in the business of ‘Energy,’” he wrote.

Earlier, at the state lunch hosted by Marcos, Trump said the two “consummated a very big trade deal.”

“It’s a fair deal for both countries and we’re very happy with that and we didn’t know that that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly,” he said.

The Philippine president’s office later said that both sides reached an understanding on areas of economic cooperation, but did not mention a trade deal, according to Reuters.

This comes after Trump said Tuesday that the U.S. and Thailand “reached substantial conclusion” in their trade negotiations.

Trump said Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports and remove substantial non-tariff barriers on a number of products as part of a trade deal the two countries will be finalizing.

He also said Thailand will be buying roughly $2.6 billion in additional U.S. agricultural products, and the deal will be finalized in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Peltola victory in Alaska completes sweeping Senate wins for Democrats
articles.summary: Mary Peltola’s projected victory in Alaska on Tuesday completes a sweeping set of Senate victories for the Democratic Party, which won every race seen as being contested on the 2026 map, as well as a few that didn’t seem in play at the beginning of the year. Democrats gained nine seats in the Senate, raising…
articles.body:
Mary Peltola’s projected victory in Alaska on Tuesday completes a sweeping set of Senate victories for the Democratic Party, which won every race seen as being contested on the 2026 map, as well as a few that didn’t seem in play at the beginning of the year.

Democrats gained nine seats in the Senate, raising their majority to 56 seats, just four short of a filibuster-proof majority.

The party had needed to gain four seats to win a majority, a number that seemed ambitious at the beginning of the year since it meant winning at least some states in which President Trump had ridden to victory in 2024.

The party ended up running way through that number, with victories in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa and Kansas. In five of those six races, the contests were seen as toss-ups on election day. But the wins didn’t end there.

Democrats also pulled off an upset win in South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Republican Darline Graham — who became the GOP nominee after the death of her brother, former Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). Few could have anticipated a Democrat representing South Carolina in the Senate just a few months ago.

Last week, Democrats added to their total with a win in Mississippi, where Scott Colom defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a tightly fought contest. Colom rode a series of creative online ads to his victory, including one that mocked Hyde-Smith for suggesting that people in Mississippi consider different proteins to deal with high beef prices. Colom’s ad suggested they try another senator.

On Tuesday, it was Alaska, another race that had been seen as a toss-up on Election Day.

With 94 percent of the vote reported, The Hill’s partner, Decision Desk HQ, projected Peltola as the winner. She held 50.12 percent of the vote to incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan’s 45.79 percent, which puts her above the 50 percent threshold to avoid ranked-choice voting coming into play.

“From Juneau to Utqiagvik, the message from Alaskans is clear: the status quo in DC is not working for Alaska,” Peltola, who will become the first Native Alaskan to serve in the Senate, said in a victory statement.

“Over the course of this campaign I’ve spoken with elders in tears about empty fish racks; families struggling to find housing they can afford; and parents in the Bush faced with the impossible choice of heating their homes or putting food on the table. Today we take a monumental step forward in addressing those issues and putting Alaska first.”

Peltola’s campaign was not without controversy.

A second Dan Sullivan ran as an independent candidate in the race, and reports, denied by Peltola’s campaign, connected it to the independent candidacy.

With the last ballot drop, Peltola held more votes than the two Dan Sullivans combined, but lawsuits over the race are a definite possibility.

That will do little to down the celebrations in Democratic circles on Wednesday, however.

The party sees the victories in states such as Alaska, South Carolina and Mississippi as locking in a Senate majority, possibly for years to come. The senators in those states and most of the others won by Democrats will hold their seats for six years, making it more difficult for Republicans to win back the Senate majority in 2028, or even 2030.

That has big implications for the final two years of Trump’s administration, as well as for the president in 2028. If a Republican wins, there’s a good chance they’ll need to deal with a Democratic Senate. If a Democrat wins, they may have a Democratic Senate to confirm nominees and judges and to work on legislation.

The election night victories included races that were toss-ups, but that doesn’t diminish the impact of some of the wins.

In Kansas, Adam Hamilton becomes the first Democrat to serve in the Senate in nearly a century. The party’s win in Texas was historic, as the Lone Star State had long been a great white whale for Democrats that was always out of reach. Democrat James Talarico rolled to a huge victory over Texas Republican Ken Paxton, and Democrats won the state’s governor’s race, too.

Democrat Josh Turek’s win in Iowa came in another state that once seemed purple, but had seemed in the Trump era to be turning increasingly red. And in Maine, a state Democrats typically win in presidential contests, the party knocked off long-time incumbent GOP Sen. Susan Collins.

Ohio was yet another state that seemed safely red in the Trump era, but former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) returned two years after a defeat to regain a Senate seat. Brown is filling out the term originally won by Vice President Vance when he served as a GOP senator from Ohio. He’ll need to run for a new term in 2028 if he wants to keep the seat.

articles.title: How the US House of Representatives chooses its leaders: A visual guide
articles.summary: After their midterm win, Democrats will lead the House from January 3. Here’s how its speaker and leaders are chosen.
articles.body:
House Democrats will vote on Wednesday to choose their leaders for the new Congress, with Hakeem Jeffries expected to win the party’s nomination for speaker. He faces no declared challenger.

If he wins the full House vote on January 3, the New York Democrat, who succeeded Nancy Pelosi as his party’s House leader in 2023, would become the first Black speaker in United States history.

His path is clear after Democrats won control of the House in the November 3 midterm elections , ending two years of Republican control under President Donald Trump. As of Wednesday, Democrats have won 257 of the House’s 435 seats and Republicans have won 171, with seven races still to be called, according to The Associated Press news agency.

In this visual guide, Al Jazeera explains the roles of the speaker, majority and minority leaders and whips, how the speaker is elected, and what happens on January 3, when power changes hands.

The House of Representatives, the lower chamber of Congress, has 435 members elected every two years. It passes laws with the Senate and controls government spending.

Each party chooses its own leaders. As the new majority, Democrats will hold the speaker’s chair and the majority posts, and Republicans will take the minority roles. The main jobs are:

Speaker: runs the House and decides which bills get a vote. Second in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president.

Majority leader: sets the House agenda and steers the majority party’s bills.

Minority leader: leads the opposition party in the House.

Whips: count votes and keep each party’s members in line.

On November 10, Republicans chose Jim Jordan of Ohio as minority leader and Tom Emmer of Minnesota as minority whip. The outgoing speaker, Mike Johnson, did not run.

On Wednesday, Democrats will also vote on the rest of their leadership team. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts is running for majority leader, which would make her the first woman to hold the post, and Pete Aguilar of California is running for majority whip.

Senate Democrats face a contested race. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Chuck Schumer, the party’s leader in the Senate since 2017, in a vote in early December.

First, each party picks its candidate in a secret ballot behind closed doors. Winning that vote makes a candidate the party’s nominee, not yet the speaker.

Then, on January 3, the full House votes, with each member saying aloud the name of their preferred candidate.

To win, a candidate needs a majority of the votes cast for a named person, which is 218 if all 435 members vote. Members who vote “present” or are absent lower that number.

If no one reaches a majority, the House votes again until someone does. Until then, it cannot swear in members or pass laws.

Most speakers win on the first ballot, but not all. In January 2023, Republican Kevin McCarthy needed 15 ballots over four days to win the job, the first time in a century that a speaker election had gone to a second ballot.

In October 2023, McCarthy also became the first speaker removed by a House vote, leaving the chamber without a speaker for three weeks.

With a large majority behind him, Jeffries is unlikely to face such a fight. Some progressives, particularly newly elected members, have withheld their support, seeking commitments on halting US military aid to Israel and on campaign finance reform. But no one has stepped forward to run against him. Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, whose petition on the party’s agenda sparked talk of a challenge, said on Monday she would not run.

Jeffries has called for a recorded vote rather than approval by acclamation, a move that will put any opposition within his party on record.

At noon (17:00 GMT) on January 3, the old Congress ends and the new one begins.

In the House chamber, in the south wing of the US Capitol, the speaker vote comes first. Once the winner is sworn in, the new speaker swears in every member at once. The House then sets its rules for the next two years, and each party’s leaders take up their posts.

In the Senate chamber, in the Capitol’s north wing, Vice President JD Vance swears in the newly elected senators. The Senate also chooses a president pro tempore, usually the majority’s most senior senator, to preside in the vice president’s absence.

The handover begins a period of divided government: a Republican president and a Democratic Congress.

Democrats will be able to block Trump’s agenda and investigate his administration. Trump can veto their bills, and overriding a veto requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers.

The date is set by the Constitution, though Congress can change it by law. In 2027, January 3 falls on a Sunday.

articles.title: Haiti must not become a war lab for China’s autonomous robot dogs
articles.summary: Haiti should not be a testing ground or a shooting range; it is a real-world setting involving real lives.
articles.body:
Last week, Salvadoran troops in Haiti conducted a military operation using robot dogs .

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele has not disclosed the robots’ manufacturer or their exact capabilities. However, artificial intelligence technology from the Chinese company Unitree , when used in conjunction with assault rifles, poses a potential danger to the civilian population. Such a development could effectively turn Haiti into a testing ground for Beijing’s warfare technology .

More than 270 non-governmental organizations across over 70 countries are promoting the Stop Killer Robots initiative, which seeks to ban — or at least regulate — autonomous systems. A machine should never have the power to decide whether a person lives or dies.

Artificial intelligence does not operate under ethical principles , and cannot distinguish between a child and a gang member, or between a weapon and a toy. Perhaps for this reason — and due to the inherent limitations and errors of AI — not many countries have deployed armed robotic dogs in actual combat against humans. They are usually implemented for exploration or rescue missions.

Communist China , which controls approximately 85 percent of the global production of AI-powered quadrupedal robots, conducted tests with armed units in Cambodia in 2024 and one simulating an invasion of Taiwan in 2025. Those were controlled exercises, not real-world conflicts involving actual human lives. In Haiti, the situation is entirely different.

In July , the Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on the importation of new humanoid and four-legged robots, citing concerns regarding cybersecurity and national security.

The Chinese government frequently subsidizes telecommunications and AI technologies, driving costs down to capture the global markets and boost technology, with both civil and military purposes.

Due to the challenges of robot technologies , armed robotic dogs in Haiti and other parts of the world could effectively become judge, jury and executioner. Transparency and temperance are required but currently are absent. Bukele’s propagandistic videos are not enough. No one knows whether the firing of weapons is controlled by the robot itself or by a human operator.

Haiti should not be a testing ground or a shooting range; it is a real-world setting involving real lives. It is a nation in crisis where gangs, self-defense groups, the United Nations, the Haitian military and police, international contractors, troops from El Salvador and civilians — all caught in the crossfire — operate. It serves as the most challenging and least regulated laboratory for testing AI-powered robots.

Haiti has welcomed Bukele’s soldiers with a mix of joy and anxiety. The man who succeeded in reducing homicide rates in what was once the most violent country in Latin America might also be able to save this failed Caribbean state — or so the hope goes.

Since late October, El Salvador has sent about 2,500 soldiers to Port-au-Prince to rescue four aviation technicians who were kidnapped by gangs. The operation received the green light from President Trump: “Do what you have to do.” However, Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressed a more cautious view, calling for strong coordination between the U.N. and Bukele’s soldiers to prevent a tragic incident of friendly fire or crossfire. Bukele has secured symbolic victories on the ground, but the primary battle is over control of the narrative.

In a matter of weeks, Bukele’s troops have recaptured the Sylvio Cator National Stadium — previously held by gangs since 2024. They have also struck the mansion headquarters of the 400 Mawozo gang. Mathias Saintil of the Boston gang has been eliminated . Wilson Joseph, the leader of 400 Mawozo, has appealed to the U.N. for help.

But while Bukele showcases his victories in Haiti on social media, no one is asking questions, providing answers, conducting investigations or raising concerns regarding the use of Chinese-made robots in Port-au-Prince.

Although the arrival of troops from El Salvador has generated hope and happiness among a desperate population, this Caribbean island must not become a testing ground for Chinese military technology. The end does not justify the means. Greater transparency and temperance are required to avert a larger tragedy.

Arturo McFields is an exiled journalist, former Nicaraguan ambassador to the Organization of American States, and a former member of the Norwegian Peace Corps. He is an alumnus of the National Defense University’s Security and Defense Seminar and the Harvard Leadership course.
