articles.body:
House Oversight Democrats sent out a dozen letters to President Trump, his family, allies and those with insight into the files tied to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, laying out their top priorities for the two years ahead.

The Wednesday letters, which request the recipient preserve all relevant documents, largely follow prior correspondence demanding the same information but nonetheless signal the top targets for the panel’s Democrats as they retake the gavel.

Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, sons of the president, were both asked about their stake in crypto ventures , while the elder brother was also asked about funding a Russian oligarch provided for his wedding.

Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner was also asked about conflicts of interest as he embarks on “business pursuits that appear to have allowed you to personally profit from your father-in-law’s presidency on a massive scale.” Kimberly Guilfoyle, previously engaged to Trump Jr., was asked about soliciting $100,000 to pay off credit card debt ahead of her ambassadorship hearing while promising access down the road.

“Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration’s self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse,” Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who is set to be the panel’s next chair, said in a statement. “These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans.”

Other letters focus on abuses with immigration enforcement as well as the Epstein files.

Vice President Vance, former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and Attorney General Todd Blanche were all asked to preserve documents related to the committee’s Epstein probe.

For Vance and Wiles, the request is primarily focused on “secret meetings inside the White House Situation Room about the Administration’s cover-up of the Epstein files and mitigating the political fallout” surrounding the tranche of documents.

For Blanche, the demand is also related to a decision to move Ghislaine Maxwell, the former girlfriend of Epstein, to a lower security prison after the two met for a discussion. Another letter was sent to the director of the Federal Bureau of Prisons and the facility where Maxwell is being held for the same line of inquiry.

On immigration, Garcia sent letters to both former Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem and her former adviser Corey Lewandowski on “abuse of DHS funds, circumventing corruption safeguards, and enriching” themselves.

For Lewandowski specifically, the California Democrat accused him of “steering lucrative government contracts toward allies.”

Both are asked about abuses within U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as was Trump’s now chief of staff Stephen Miller, with the committee referring to him as the “‘linchpin’ and ‘architect’ of the Trump administration’s most extreme policies.”

Finally, a letter to Caroline Townsend asks about her role leading the Trust for the National Mall, saying the organization is “acting as a middleman by taking in hundreds of millions of dollars in donations” to fund the president’s White House ballroom construction.

Many of those donations come from those with business before the government.

The letter cites embattled company Nvidia as one such example, noting it donated millions “shortly after receiving permission from the Trump Administration to sell advanced microchips to the People’s Republic of China, as well as a favorable decision from the Department of Commerce closing an investigation into the company.”

articles.title: Escaping chaos at home, Trump’s Asia tour is shaping up to be a disaster
articles.summary: Trump’s unserious welcome in Manila set the tone for an unserious foreign trip that seems more like an effort to escape the humiliation of a bruising midterm election loss than an attempt at real diplomacy.
articles.body:
When a president visits a foreign nation on official business, it is traditional to greet him with a local rendition of “Hail to the Chief” or “The Star-Spangled Banner.” Not so for President Trump, our most untraditional of presidents.

As Trump touched down at Ninoy Aquino Airport in Manila on Tuesday for the first day of his whirlwind trip to Asia, Philippine officials instead greeted him with a rousing orchestral version of the 1978 disco hit “YMCA.” The tune is a well-known Trump favorite, though perhaps not the first thing jet-lagged staffers wanted to hear after an 18-hour flight.

Trump’s unserious welcome in Manila set the tone for an unserious foreign trip that seems more like an effort to escape the humiliation of a bruising midterm election loss than an attempt at real diplomacy. The visit also puts Trump conveniently abroad as his feckless lackeys at Homeland Security and the Transportation Department continue to botch the administration’s response to a multi-day string of major cyber-outages that grounded more than 20,000 domestic flights and briefly took the nation’s largest bank offline .

But while Trump has been able to duck most of the fallout from the nation’s cyber-instability, he couldn’t resist making the situation worse for Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. When asked by a reporter if he was concerned about the recent outages, Trump flippantly dismissed the chaos while also suggesting that the service disruptions at Microsoft, Chase and the Federal Aviation Administration were targeted cyberattacks.

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful, and you have all the money, things like that happen,” Trump said . “It’s fine.”

It sure sounds like Trump is implying that America has become a target of cyberattacks due to its wealth and power, and his cavalier attitude doesn’t inspire confidence that he takes those threats seriously. His explanation is also miles away from the shifting excuses given by Duffy and Mullin, who blamed a combination of faulty routers and inept construction workers for Friday’s emergency ground stop.

Trump’s explanation sounds more like foreign malice than domestic error, and it’s yet another reminder that the American people should exercise caution in trusting anything his administration says. Whether they are engaging in knowing lies or bumbling about through sheer incompetence, no one in the White House seems to know exactly what is going on.

Even with the benefit of distance from the digital meltdown at home, Trump still managed to rack up his own political embarrassments almost immediately.

Officials hastily scrapped a planned meeting to sign a trade deal with Thailand — Trump’s only major event that day — after Thai officials stressed that the agreement hadn’t been finalized. Instead, Trump and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul signed an empty “joint statement agreement” that merely announced a future announcement. The only thing holding the event back from true Trumpian meaninglessness was the absence of a promise to have the deal done “ in two weeks .”

Trump’s foreign side quests pale in comparison to the importance of his upcoming trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin , where he’s expected to discuss the war in Ukraine and the increasingly tense AI arms race between the U.S. and China. Yet Trump is entering those discussions with a shockingly weak hand and bitter divisions on China policy splitting his administration.

The revelation that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick allegedly resisted efforts to restrict the Singapore-based tech firm Megaspeed from buying Nvidia’s advanced AI chips has set up a brutal battle with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who blames Lutnick for those chips falling into Chinese hands. Lutnick’s shocking decision to ignore Trump’s direct orders appears to have left the president stunned and his administration paralyzed on how to move forward. Instead of projecting confidence, the normally boastful Trump telegraphed uncertainty and weakness in remarks to reporters before departing on his trip.

“If you did do something, you could have a blow-up with China,” Trump said . “We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it.”

Back in September, Trump walked into a meeting with Xi without a clear strategy for what he hoped to gain. The result was little more than a photo-op summit that foreign policy experts widely regarded as a failure that strengthened Xi’s hand domestically while allowing the Chinese leader to stall for time on issues like AI and regional security.

Trump is now walking into an even more important meeting with Xi and Putin, and he’s doing so from an even weaker and more conflicted position than he did in September. This time, he risks giving two of the world’s most repressive autocrats the upper hand in a conflict that could decide the fate of Ukraine and the future of American global leadership.

Max Burns is a veteran Democratic strategist and founder of Third Degree Strategies.

articles.title: USCIS delays are making immigrants illegal
articles.summary: No one should lose the right to live and work in this country because the government failed to do its own job in a timely fashion.
articles.body:
Galina Bobreneva did everything the law asks of a married immigrant. She applied for a green card in December 2025 through her husband, a U.S. citizen and a Trump supporter. Then she waited. In July, Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained her for 16 days, and she was released only after posting a $35,000 bond. Her green card application is still pending.

Her case is not an aberration. It is what happens when a government slow to approve paperwork becomes fast to detain the people waiting on it.

According to its own website, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services field offices now take nearly seven years to decide a green card petition filed by a citizen for a spouse, parent or child under 21. A citizen who files today might wait until 2033. More than 572,000 such petitions are pending. Green card holders petitioning for adult sons and daughters face a wait of over 15 years , and that is before the additional time it takes to schedule a visa appointment at a U.S. consulate abroad.

These delays reach well beyond family cases. By July, a record 12.8 million cases were pending. Investors seeking to put money into American companies wait 36 months . Some applicants for work permits wait 16 months . Over the past 18 months, processing times rose in 14 of the agency’s 17 categories .

For many immigrants, a long wait is not just an inconvenience; it is a legal hazard. USCIS ended the automatic 540-day extension of work permits for renewal applications filed after Oct. 30, 2025. As of June 30, more than 432,000 renewal applications had been pending for at least six months, including more than 91,000 pending for over 18 months . Those applicants risk losing work authorization, and with it, lawful status, even though they followed all the rules.

That matters because, by the agency’s own account , filing an application does not make someone legal. Pending applicants have been arrested at the very appointments the government scheduled for them. A Peruvian was detained at a USCIS interview despite a pending marriage-based green card application. A 60-year-old woman who had lived here for more than 30 years was detained at a biometric appointment tied to her pending green card application.

Why are the delays growing? Four forces are at work.

First, USCIS has reassigned officers from deciding petitions to investigating alleged fraud , including in previously approved cases. Fewer adjudicators are left to work through the pending ones. USCIS has always had fraud investigators, but the current focus on fraud in every petition has created an imbalance in agency resources.

Second, USCIS no longer gives deference to its own prior approvals. Routine extensions that once moved quickly now require fresh scrutiny, slowing the entire system.

Third, experienced USCIS adjudicators were fired or took early retirement because of the Department of Government Efficiency.

Fourth, and whatever the intent, the slowdown serves the administration’s goal of curbing legal immigration. It also expands the pool of people available for ICE to detain and deport. Delay converts the paperwork process into an enforcement pipeline .

Imagine if the Internal Revenue Service took four years to issue refunds, or if the Social Security Administration left retirees waiting a decade for their checks. Americans would be furious, and Congress would act. Immigration delays deserve the same outrage, because the people harmed include U.S. citizens: spouses separated for years, employers unable to keep workers, families living in limbo.

Congress has several tools. It can hold oversight hearings to find out where the bottleneck lies. It can set statutory deadlines for deciding petitions, as it has for other agencies. And it can redirect a portion of the tens of billions of dollars it gave ICE to USCIS, which is largely funded by applicant fees and has little leeway to hire.

No one should lose the right to live and work in this country because the government failed to do its own job in a timely fashion. A nation that prides itself on the rule of law should not punish people for waiting patiently in the line it built.

Stephen Yale-Loehr is a retired professor of immigration law practice at Cornell Law School.

articles.title: House Democrats tap Ted Lieu as caucus chairman
articles.summary: House Democrats on Wednesday elected Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) to be the caucus chairman in the next Congress, elevating, once again, a figure who is already the highest-ranking Asian American in the history of the lower chamber. Lieu was running for the seat unchallenged, and the vote, by acclamation, kicked off the Democrats’ leadership elections…
articles.body:
House Democrats on Wednesday elected Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) to be the caucus chairman in the next Congress, elevating, once again, a figure who is already the highest-ranking Asian American in the history of the lower chamber.

Lieu was running for the seat unchallenged, and the vote, by acclamation, kicked off the Democrats’ leadership elections in the wake of their stunning midterm victory earlier in the month.

As chairman, Lieu is the fourth-ranking House Democrat, but his election came first because the caucus chairman presides over the remaining contests, which are scheduled to take place over the course of Wednesday and Thursday.

Like Lieu, the other top Democrats are running uncontested, meaning there will almost certainly be no shakeups in the top tiers of the party brass.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is expected to become the Speaker in the next Congress. Rep. Katherine Clark (Mass.), the Democratic whip, is poised to rise to the majority leader spot. And Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), the current caucus chairman, is on track to replace Clark as the whip.

That leadership team has been in place since 2023, when former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) and her longtime deputies stepped down from the leadership ranks to clear a path for a younger generation of leaders.

Lieu, an Air Force veteran, has served as vice chairman of the caucus over the same duration. Along with Aguilar, he’s been on the front lines of the Democrats’ messaging strategy, which proved successful in the midterms and gave a boost to the entire leadership team.

Lieu has also been one of the key congressional players in the debate over artificial intelligence, which is creating enormous challenges for lawmakers as they grapple with how — or even whether — to regulate the industry amid warnings that it poses a threat, not only to jobs, but to the future of humanity.

Lieu said this month that he’ll continue that work in the next Congress, promising legislation designed to rein in the AI industry — a process he said was neglected while Republicans controlled both chambers and the White House over the past two years.

“That’s going to take a little bit of time as we have this new caucus, and you have to set up the committees, and then you have to pass the legislation,” he said this month. “But you’re going to see that occur in a way that did not occur this term.”

articles.title: FAA chief defends $50B funding ask amid bipartisan skepticism from Congress
articles.summary: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) chief Bryan Bedford acknowledged the “whiplash” in Congress Wednesday after the Trump administration’s $50 billion funding request toward his agency but asserted the boost is needed to upgrade air travel infrastructure “right.” Bedford — who was on Capitol Hill after the FAA called a rare nationwide ground stop last week —…
articles.body:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) chief Bryan Bedford acknowledged the “whiplash” in Congress Wednesday after the Trump administration’s $50 billion funding request toward his agency but asserted the boost is needed to upgrade air travel infrastructure “right.”

Bedford — who was on Capitol Hill after the FAA called a rare nationwide ground stop last week — defended Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s calls during The Hill’s “Red, Flight and Blue: The Future of Aviation” event Wednesday, co-sponsored by Airlines for America.

“We sent a letter to the Hill on Thursday, asking for 30 billion, and then sending out the letter yesterday asking for 50 billion,” Bedford said. “So, I think there’s some indigestion associated with that, and I understand that.”

He went on to address concerns surrounding how the FAA plans to use the additional funds, asserting the agency pushed all appropriated money from its 2026 budget toward upgrades — despite the fact a “tiny amount” has been spent.

Bedford said the notion the FAA is not spending the money it has is “ridiculous” and that the boost would help the agency finish the job — before clarifying air traffic control system issues are an ongoing issue.

“We can go through the inspector general reports and the Congressional Budget Office reports. They’ve been reporting for over 30 years on how unsustainable the system is, and we have continued to patch it and duct tape it and kick the can down the road,” Bedford said.

The administrator made argued air travel is crucial to the U.S. economy and that updating the system would create a “robust economic opportunity.” He attributed this call of action to President Trump.

“If we’re going to fix the system, we’re going to return it to the hold standard,” Bedford said. “Let’s do it right, let’s fix all of it.”

Bedford said Trump in his first term attempted to fix the air traffic control system, but the effort fizzled due to arguments as to who will pay for it and debates as to whether to privatize the government function. He said Wednesday these argument needs to end.

“I implore everybody, stop arguing about who pays for it because tax patterns pay for it. Even if we raise landing fees or we raise ticket taxes, that is a tax on consumers,” Bedford said.

Rep. Dina Titus (D-Nev.), a member of the House Aviation subcommittee, hit Duffy during Wednesday’s event for making a public funding request without explaining how the administration would spend the money. She highlighted Congress already appropriated billions for the infrastructure update.

“What happened to the other money that we’ve already given you through the big beautiful bill and through the bipartisan infrastructure bill? What have you done with that?” she told The Hill’s Sarah Fortinsky, referencing what lawmakers are asking.

Rep. Steve Womack (R-Ark.), who chairs the House Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and Related Agencies committee, also voiced skepticism on whether there is a path to passing the $50 million dollar request.

articles.body:

Alsobrooks announced her support for Schumer Wednesday during the Bethesda-Chevy Chase Democratic Breakfast Club, according to The Baltimore Banner.

Alsobrooks revealed that she met with Schumer and committed to support him before Van Hollen jumped into the leadership race.

“I do support Chris as a colleague and everything but I am definitely a person of my word,” she told the Montgomery County Democrats, adding that she “made a commitment” to Schumer.

Alsobrooks had kept her support for Schumer secret up until now.

When asked Monday whom she would support the leadership race, Alsobrooks answered: “We’ll see.”

Many other Democrats are keeping their preference in the race secret though Schumer allies expect more than 40 votes for Schumer to be re-elected leader in December.

Van Hollen says he has commitments from 15 Democrats, though only four have announced their support for his leadership bid publicly. Those four are Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.

Fifteen Senate Democrats have now publicly pledged their support for Schumer. (This doesn’t include Schumer himself.)

articles.title: Beyond the airport: Today’s aviation security must evolve to prevent modern threats
articles.summary: As the holiday season approaches, congested flight schedules and packed airplanes will challenge already strained security operations at America’s airports. Aviation security must extend beyond the checkpoint.
articles.body:
Air travel has been the safest mode of transportation for decades. The Federal Aviation Administration and the Transportation Security Administration both play critical roles in keeping it that way. Last week’s nationwide air system shutdown highlights why safety is always the primary concern, as several other recent events raise questions about whether aviation risks are changing — and whether security policies are keeping pace.

The incident on the FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv in late September, where a co-pilot attempted to take control of an airplane and fly it into Israel’s main airport passenger terminal, highlights the problem of insider threats. This has placed a spotlight on pilots, underscoring the need for comprehensive background vetting of anyone in control of an airplane.

Then there is the improvised explosive device found in a men’s room trash can at the George Bush Houston Intercontinental Airport on the anniversary of the 9/11 attacks. Given that this IED was discovered on the sterile side of the airport, questions remain about how it entered without detection.

Security breaches around airport perimeters , which occur around two to three times per month , on average, have also been in the news. While most prove to be harmless intrusions, one recent breach at Denver International Airport led to the perpetrator being struck by a Frontier airplane during takeoff. The TSA’s emphasis on airport security checkpoints makes sense, given the risk calculus; however, focusing so heavily on them may leave perimeter vulnerabilities with insufficient attention.

As disturbing as all these risks may sound, drone warfare in Russia’s war with Ukraine and the Middle East conflict suggests that drone attacks around airports may be a growing threat . The FAA receives around 100 reports of unauthorized drones around U.S. airports every month. The presence of drones, particularly when airplanes take off or land, poses a threat to air safety that will only increase with time and cannot be ignored. Last month’s Houthi attack at the Riyadh airport demonstrates that aviation infrastructure remains a prime target for terrorist attacks.

TSA Administrator David P. Cummins earlier this year introduced the Horizon 25 Strategy to enhance aviation security across multiple dimensions. Though drone risks are mentioned, TSA investments continue to focus heavily on airport screening lanes, including the deployment of computed tomography machines for carry-on bags, which may eventually lead to a relaxation of the agency’s 3-1-1 liquids restriction .

While airport security checkpoints are the most obvious avenue to introducing threats into the air system, they are by no means the only one.

The TSA has pulled back on several initiatives when new programs were reassessed and found not to provide ample levels of security or value. For example, it terminated the Gold+ program in August, shifting focus back to the Screening Partnership Program , which centers exclusively on privatizing airport screening personnel. It also paused the expansion of the Gateside by TSA’s PreCheck program, leaving the 13 pilot airports in place.

Limited resources constrain efforts to address other aviation-security threats. Checkpoints consume around 70 percent of the TSA budget , and for good reason — they screen around 2.5 million passengers every day on average , acting as both a barrier and a deterrent against known threats. The problem is that screening lanes are also bottlenecks, encouraging those with malicious intent to look for less-guarded pathways to cause harm and disruption. Identifying ways to redirect such resources without compromising security is challenging, but necessary.

When my research helped lay the groundwork for risk-based screening and TSA PreCheck, the goal was to focus scarce resources on unknown threats. One way to achieve this today is by incentivizing more travelers to enroll in trusted traveler programs like TSA PreCheck and Global Entry, perhaps even exploring ways to offer them at no cost to some travelers willing to undergo the required background check. The Horizon 25 program hopes to add 20 million more people to PreCheck over the next three years.

Expanding voluntary passenger vetting has multiple benefits. It reduces system risk and permits more people to use expedited screening lanes that are faster to traverse and reduce passenger waiting times. These lanes also require fewer TSA personnel and less expensive technologies to operate. Expanding participation offers a cost-effective way to free up resources for emerging threats that cannot be mitigated at airport checkpoints.

As the holiday season approaches, congested flight schedules and packed airplanes will challenge already strained security operations. The risk may be small in absolute terms, but the consequences are enormous. Preparing for well-known threats remains necessary, but it is no longer sufficient. Aviation security must extend beyond the checkpoint, with resources allocated to protect the entire system.

Sheldon H. Jacobson, Ph.D., is a professor of Computer Science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He applies his expertise in data-driven risk-based decision-making to evaluate and inform public policy. His research on risk-based security laid the foundation for TSA Precheck.

articles.title: Evans planning return to Congress with bid for Boebert seat
articles.summary: Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colo.) will mount a comeback bid for a separate House seat in Colorado after losing reelection, he announced earlier this week. “Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls’ sports and locker rooms,…
articles.body:
Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colo.) will mount a comeback bid for a separate House seat in Colorado after losing reelection , he announced earlier this week.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls’ sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans wrote on social platform X .

Evans lost reelection to Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel (D) in Colorado’s 8th Congressional District by a nearly 15-point margin. President Trump carried the suburban Denver district by nearly 2 points in 2024, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s election partner.

The outgoing lawmaker is now turning to the Centennial State’s 4th Congressional District, a vast, GOP-leaning area that takes up much of Eastern Colorado. But even the 4th district succumbed to the strong Democratic performance this cycle after Rep. Lauren Boebert (R) lost to Democrat Eileen Laubacher by just over 3,000 votes.

If Evans does successfully mount a comeback in 2028, it would continue recent district-switching efforts Colorado Republicans have attempted to stay in Congress.

Boebert nearly lost reelection in the 3rd Congressional District — a GOP-leaning district encompassing much of Western Colorado — holding on in 2022 by just over 500 votes. After her opponent in that race announced he would run a second, well-funded campaign against her, she opted to run in the 4th district instead.

The chair of the Colorado Republican Party said at the time that he thought it was “not the best move.”

The move paid off in 2024, but not in 2026. The Republican who succeeded her in the 3rd district, Rep. Jeff Hurd, is now the only remaining congressional Republican in the state.

Boebert said she will not run again in 2028, according to KKTV, leaving a path for Evans to be the GOP nominee.

Evans defeated an incumbent Democrat in 2024 by a narrow margin. In Monday post online, he defended the decision to switch districts, claiming ties to counties in the 4th district.

“I’m a Colorado native, born in Arapahoe County, raised in Elbert and Douglas Counties, a four-year letterman at Kiowa High School, and currently own and operate a small farm in Weld County,” Evans wrote. “I know the suburban challenges facing Colorado too, … watching the population of the Denver Metro area and Northern Colorado double in my lifetime.”

The 8th and 4th districts border one another, and split Weld, Adams and Larimer counties, according to DDHQ, three suburban Denver counties.

articles.title: New York Times knocks ‘tired’ White House attack on Haberman

Responding to a story about comments Haberman made about former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, a spokesperson for President Trump said the reporter has…
articles.body:
The New York Times is defending Maggie Haberman, one of its star reporters, from a new attack coming from the White House over her reporting on the Trump administration.

Responding to a story about comments Haberman made about former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, a spokesperson for President Trump said the reporter has a “creepy obsession” with Trump and “clings” to him for “relevance and money.”

The Times, in a pointed statement of its own , stood by Haberman.

“She is an exemplary journalist whose deeply sourced, consequential reporting has informed millions of Americans about vital decisions made by those in power,” the outlet said in its statement. “This is a tired attempt to belittle a journalist for doing her job, in retaliation for coverage the administration doesn’t like.”

Haberman and Trump have had a rocky relationship dating back to his time as a real estate mogul in New York City.

She is considered one of the nation’s leading political reporters and has penned books about Trump’s rise to power in the U.S. and his legacy in American history.

Trump has repeatedly attacked the Times and called out Haberman by name over her reporting, recently suing the outlet over its coverage of his reelection campaign.

articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said he is doing his best to whip votes for Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s (D-Md.) challenge against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in the race to lead the party in the majority.

“I’m doing my best. I think, you know, I’ve known Chuck Schumer for years. I like Chuck, but I think there has not been the sense of urgency that we have needed to address the enormous, enormous crises facing working families in this country,” Sanders told host Chris Hayes on MS NOW’s “All In” Tuesday evening.

The Vermont senator continued that he believed the issues facing the U.S. are “unprecedented in modern history,” including “a handful of people with incredible wealth and power,” thus warranting a leadership change.

“We need a sense of urgency. We need to stand with the American people and, frankly, have the guts,” Sanders said. “Not too many people talk about this, to take on the big money in the Republican Party and in the Democratic Party.”

Sanders announced his support for Van Hollen’s bid for Senate leadership on Nov. 10, following other progressive lawmakers signaling their support for the Maryland Democrat. Though, the senior senator from New York declared Tuesday he already had enough votes to win majority leader.

As of Wednesday morning, The Hill’s whip list counted 15 senators who publicly backed Schumer.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes, and we’re all going to roll up our sleeves, and we’re going to focus on lowering costs, ending corruption. Those are the things we’re focused on,” Schumer told reporters.

Van Hollen stated Sunday he had the backing of 15 senators, though only four lawmakers have publicly supported his candidacy, per the whip list. He has also accused Schumer of inflating support in the Senate , saying multiple senators who the minority leader’s team said would vote for him have vowed privately to support the Maryland Democrat instead.

“There’s a hunger for change within the Senate Democratic caucus,” Van Hollen said. “This really is a response to the call of voters, who clearly rejected Donald Trump and his awful policies. But they haven’t fully hired Democrats.”

Van Hollen has campaigned for Senate majority leader on his progressive stances — calling out Schumer for allegedly working with special interests tied to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and cryptocurrency.

Of the 33 undecided senators, many are calling for a caucus debate, with progressive and centrist Senate Democrats shying away from showing their support.

Vice President Vance will not appear at The New York Times’s annual DealBook summit as the country grapples with ongoing tech outages plaguing major companies and services in recent days.

During the summit on Wednesday, Times journalist Andrew Ross Sorkin announced that Vance had abruptly canceled a planned appearance and noted the ongoing outages.

A series of incidents involving major government and private sector digital systems in recent days has led to widespread concern about national security and advancements in artificial intelligence.

President Trump, who is in China meeting with world leaders, when asked downplayed the outages, saying he does not take responsibility for a nationwide airline ground stop Friday and that services going down are “fine.”

A number of conservative media personalities and GOP lawmakers have questioned explanations given by government officials for the outages, which officials have chalked up to routine maintenance or failed tech upgrades.

Vance yesterday attempted to calm Americans during a Fox News appearance, saying “a lot of my friends have reached out asking if they should prepare to build a bunker or stock up on food and water.”

“My answer to that is no,” the vice president said . “We don’t see a crisis coming down. But you have to be prepared for everything.”

articles.title: GOP chair blasts Patel for skipping worldwide threats hearing
articles.summary: FBI Director Kash Patel was blasted by Rep. Andrew Garbarino (R-N.Y.), the chair of the House Homeland Security Committee, for his “refusal” to testify by skipping an appearance for the annual worldwide threats hearing. “Today’s hearing date was first provided to Director Patel in August. There was no surprise or last-minute request, and despite repeated…
articles.body:
FBI Director Kash Patel was blasted by Rep. Andrew Garbarino (R-N.Y.), the chair of the House Homeland Security Committee, for his “refusal” to testify by skipping an appearance for the annual worldwide threats hearing.

“Today’s hearing date was first provided to Director Patel in August. There was no surprise or last-minute request, and despite repeated attempts over the span of several months between then and now to find any date when he could testify, the director made clear that he had no intention of appearing,” Garbarino said in his opening remarks.

“Director Patel’s refusal to testify marks a significant departure from well-established committee precedent,” he added, noting that Patel’s predecessor Christopher Wray testified before the panel six times for the hearing.

Scheduled regularly over the last decade, the hearing is convened to allow the public to hear from the Homeland Security Secretary, the head of the FBI, and the director of national intelligence about threats facing the homeland.

At the Wednesday hearing, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton were in attendance.

Christopher Raia, a longtime agent now serving as the deputy director of the FBI, attended in Patel’s place.

An FBI official told The Hill that Patel was in the field this week visiting office across four different states.

“The FBI designated Deputy Director Raia for this hearing and notified the committee several weeks ago — and Deputy Director Raia is a career agent with over 20 years’ experience at every level of the Bureau,” the official said.

Garbarino thanked Raia for appearing but argued the hearing was the director’s responsibility.

“The committee has been clear in its direct communications to the FBI and through his historical record, that this is a hearing where the FBI director is expected to participate on behalf of the bureau. Our focus on worldwide threats transcends politics, and the director should be here to brief Congress,” the chair said.

Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.), the top Democrat on the panel set to serve as chair next year, also knocked Patel.

“Director Patel’s absence for a second consecutive year limits the committee’s ability to conduct effective oversight at this hearing. Director Patel is shirking his responsibility to appear before this committee, just as he has shirked his responsibilities leading the nation’s premier federal law enforcement agency,” he said.

“Mr. Chairman, you should take it as an affront that the director finds time to spend taxpayers’ dollars flying to his girlfriend’s concert, go VIP snorkeling at a Pearl Harbor memorial site, celebrate with hockey teams, and intimidate journalists for reporting what he doesn’t like, but has no time to testify before this committee.”

articles.title: US measles progress has officially reversed, and children are paying the price
articles.summary: Reversing course requires action across the public health system.
articles.body:
Earlier this year, my colleague and I warned that turmoil in U.S. vaccine policy was increasing the risk of a measles resurgence. We did not want to be proven correct.

Yesterday, the Pan American Health Organization formally announced that measles is no longer eliminated in the United States. Children are getting sick, families are facing grief and uncertainty and a fearsome disease previously tamed is spreading again.

This was preventable. Before a measles vaccine was licensed in 1963, an estimated 3 million to 4 million Americans contracted measles each year. Hundreds died, tens of thousands were hospitalized and some children suffered permanent brain damage.

Decades of vaccination and public health campaigns changed that. In 2000, the United States eliminated endemic measles transmission. Imported cases and occasional outbreaks continued, but high vaccination coverage and effective public health systems prevented sustained transmission.

This achievement also protected people who could not yet be vaccinated, particularly infants. Babies generally receive their first routine measles, mumps and rubella or MMR vaccine dose at 12 to 15 months , so their protection depends partly on the immunity of those around them. High community vaccination coverage helped shield them from exposure.

For 26 years, American children grew up without continuous measles transmission. I raised my children here during that time and remain profoundly grateful they had protection built by scientists, clinicians and public health professionals that generations of parents could not take for granted. It is devastating that today’s families face the loss of an achievement we worked so hard to secure.

The consequences are already here. As of Nov. 12, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had reported 5,412 confirmed cases and 591 hospitalizations already this year. State authorities have reported at least 10 deaths, although the CDC’s published tally lists only six . This discrepancy raises important questions about the transparency of national reporting. The public should not have to reconcile conflicting numbers to understand the scale of an outbreak. Even one of these deaths is too many.

Babies too young to be vaccinated, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems — including those undergoing chemotherapy — face particular risks . Clinicians are confronting cases and complications they may rarely have encountered, including measles in pregnant women and infants infected before birth. The parents of infants should not have to worry that taking an unvaccinated baby to the pediatrician or running errands could expose them to a serious disease.

We have a safe, effective way to prevent measles: Two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97 percent effective . So why are we here? Because misinformation and declining confidence in public health agencies have contributed to falling vaccination coverage.

Historic trends predate the current administration, and responsibility cannot be assigned to one individual. But as Health and Human Services secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has significant responsibility for what happens next: restoring confidence in vaccination, strengthening public health protections and ensuring that policy is guided by scientific evidence.

Under Kennedy, the entire Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which advises the CDC on vaccine recommendations, was replaced. Changes to the committee and its processes raise serious questions about how scientific evidence is evaluated and incorporated into national policy. Vaccine recommendations affect millions of people and must be grounded in rigorous scientific review, transparent decision-making and qualified expert advice.

We also track measles because it is the canary in the coal mine. The resurgence of measles — one of the most contagious infectious diseases known — is an early warning about the wider state of U.S. infectious disease prevention. The same weaknesses that allow measles to spread will leave communities vulnerable to other infectious disease threats.

Preventing and controlling outbreaks requires much more than a vaccine. Health departments need capacity to identify cases, investigate outbreaks, trace contacts and reach people who have been exposed. Clinicians need timely information and guidance. Laboratories need resources to test samples. Communities need accurate, trusted communication. These activities depend on coordination across federal, state and local government, and on a skilled public health workforce.

Yet these are precisely the capacities weakened by recent workforce reductions and funding cuts. Public health systems cannot be expected to respond effectively when the people and infrastructure they depend on have been weakened.

Reversing course requires action across the public health system. Federal and state leaders must communicate clearly about vaccination, counter misinformation and protect access to immunization. Congress must provide sustained funding for health departments, laboratories and outbreak response. The CDC and other scientific institutions must maintain independent, transparent, evidence-based decision-making. Leaders must ensure that the public health workforce has the resources and institutional support to perform its functions.

Children should not suffer from a disease we know how to prevent. Families should not experience devastating and preventable loss. Parents should not have to question the protections they grew up trusting. And the public health workforce should not have to fight with one hand tied behind its back to protect communities.

Policymakers at every level have a responsibility to act.

Katie D. Schenk, MSc Ph.D. is a former health scientist and senior service fellow at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. She edits The Public Health Workforce is Not OK newsletter and leads KDS Public Health Consulting LLC .

articles.title: Dems put Jeffries one step closer to Speakership — and the history books
articles.summary: House Democrats on Wednesday nominated Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to become the next House Speaker, putting the Brooklyn native one step closer to entering the history books as the first Black lawmaker to hold the gavel. The tally was a lopsided 251-11, affirming Jeffries’s popularity within the caucus and setting the stage for him to…
articles.body:
House Democrats on Wednesday nominated Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to become the next House Speaker, putting the Brooklyn native one step closer to entering the history books as the first Black lawmaker to hold the gavel.

The tally was a lopsided 251-11, affirming Jeffries’s popularity within the caucus and setting the stage for him to win the Speakership in the next phase of the two-step process, which will occur on Jan. 3 with a vote of the full House on the chamber floor.

The outcome was no surprise. Jeffries ran uncontested, and the vast majority of Democrats had lined up behind him heading into the closed-door vote. The blue wave that crashed into the midterms gave Jeffries a boost, providing him with ammunition to claim a popular vision — and an enormous cushion to absorb defectors.

Still, some Democrats have also questioned Jeffries’s leadership record in the first two years of President Trump’s second term, saying he simply didn’t fight hard enough to counter the administration as it stretched the limits of executive power in its approach to immigration enforcement, the Iran war, government spending and a host of other issues. Some outside liberal groups have spent the weeks since the midterms scrambling to recruit a more liberal alternative. None emerged.

Still, Jeffries took nothing for granted heading into Wednesday’s vote. He took pains to huddle with all the various ideological groups within the diverse caucus, from the left-wing Progressive Caucus to the centrist Blue Dogs. And he also met with a long list of Democrats in the incoming freshman class, which includes some of his most public critics.

Amid the grumbling, Jeffries took the unusual step of calling for his nomination to be decided by recorded vote. That was a last-minute twist — and an unexpected one, since he faced no challenger, and the other leaders are likely to be promoted by fast-track votes of acclamation. Many thought Jeffries would do the same.

But the recorded tally allowed Jeffries to gauge precisely how much support he has heading into the Speaker vote of the full House on Jan. 3, when the bar for success will be much higher. While he needed just a simple majority of Democrats to win the Speaker’s nomination, he will need 218 votes on the floor to secure the gavel early next year.

Wednesday’s vote was by closed ballot, meaning Democrats were free to make their choice anonymously. The final count is a demonstration that, despite some criticism, Jeffries has the overwhelming support of his troops heading into Jan. 3 — and the last two years of the Trump presidency.

Shortly before Jeffries’s nomination, House Democrats voted to promote Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) to chair of the House Democratic Caucus, a step up from the vice chair seat he’s held over the past four years.

Jeffries’s top deputies — Reps. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) and Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) — also kept their positions of power in Wednesday’s elections, rising to majority leader and Democratic whip, respectively.

That team has been in place since 2023, when former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) and her long-time lieutenants — Reps. Steny Hoyer (D-Md.) and James Clyburn (D-S.C.) — stepped out of the top leadership ranks to clear the field for a younger crop of rising stars in the party.

Jeffries already made history during that process, becoming the first Black lawmaker to lead either party in either chamber. His ascension to Speaker would mark another chapter, putting him second in line to the presidency and making him the de facto leader of the national Democratic Party, at least until a 2028 presidential nominee emerges.

Jeffries is already forecasting some of the issues he intends to prioritize next year. The early list features efforts to reverse Medicaid cuts adopted by Republicans last year and expand ObamaCare tax credits, which Republicans allowed to expire at the start of 2026.

Jeffries is also vowing to focus intently on accountability amid numerous accounts of administration officials using their power to advance personal interests. Democrats are already planning a long list of investigations into Trump, his Cabinet, his family and other allies as a first order of business next year, setting the stage for an explosive clash between the White House and Congress under the newly divided government.

Jeffries will have his share of challenges, however. The midterms have elevated the number of centrist Democrats, who hail from purple districts and are advocating for moderate policies that can win bipartisan support and become law. They will clash with the liberal wing of the caucus, which also boosted its numbers and wants to adopt progressive priorities, including “ Medicare for All ” and the end of military aid to Israel.

Jeffries and his leadership team will be caught in the middle of those competing groups.

articles.title: Democrats boycott Senate hearing over frustration with Trump nominations
articles.summary: Senate Democrats on the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee did not appear at a scheduled committee meeting Wednesday morning, citing their opposition to a nominee for the Federal Communications Commission that Republicans planned to vote on. “All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans…
articles.body:
Senate Democrats on the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee did not appear at a scheduled committee meeting Wednesday morning, citing their opposition to a nominee for the Federal Communications Commission that Republicans planned to vote on.

“All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans and rushing nominees through the Committee process in this lame duck session with no Democratic pairs,” read a statement from the Democrats on the panel.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), the panel’s chairman, said at the opening of the meeting that the Democrats were protesting the nominee, Danielle Thumann Severs, because Trump had not nominated a Democratic commissioner alongside her.

Cruz said the Democrats on the panel had sent him a letter urging him to postpone Thumann Severs’ nomination process because Democrats were anticipating holding the gavel in January.

Republicans strongly criticized Democrats for the boycott.

“Candidly, it’s a terrible harbinger heading into next year,” said Cruz. “What it should tell all of us is the Democrats have zero intention of processing any of the president’s nominees. We are heading into two years of total obstruction, total war, partisan warfare is what the Democrats are promising us.”

“For those of you who voted for Democrats, what did you vote for? Did you vote for people who don’t show up for work?” said Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio).

Democrats had been calling for Thumann Severs’ nomination to be pulled from the meeting because they did not want to confirm “controversial nominees” during the lame duck before Democrats take the majority in the new Congress.

Republicans voted anyway on the nominations, including Thumann Severs’, and she was advanced out of committee.

Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kansas) noted he had spoken with Thumann Severs on Wednesday morning and she had reiterated her commitment to protecting political free speech on the airwaves, something he was concerned about the FCC over-regulating, but that he was still expecting her to meet with him before the full floor vote.

Fox News’s Laura Ingraham, in an…
articles.body:
Fox News’s Brian Kilmeade slammed Vice President Vance over the Iran war on Tuesday and said he “never should have been vice president.”

On Monday, Vance pledged that the U.S. would not make a long-term commitment to the war in Iran compared with prior American conflicts in the region.

Fox News’s Laura Ingraham, in an interview with Vance, told him he was facing blame for the memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Iran not working for Republicans before their dramatic midterm losses. The vice president defended President Trump and said he still had “a lot of options.”

“My prediction, Laura, is that whatever the president ultimately decides to do, there are going to be people who demand more, who want the war to go on indefinitely,” Vance told Ingraham.

“And what I feel quite confident about the president of the United States, and again, there’s no daylight here, is that whatever he ultimately decides to do, however he ultimately decides to bring the conflict to a close, he is not going to let this become a forever war,” he added.

In response to Vance’s comments on the war, Kilmeade lashed out at the vice president.

“There is not one person that I have ever met, that wants an endless war, who will say, ‘The president’s got to keep fighting no matter what,’” the Fox News host said on his radio show.

“Win, neutralize our 40-year enemy and you end it when you want to end it. It’s not that people are never going to be satisfied. So that is another straw man argument that this guy puts up. I’m talking about the vice president of the United States, he never should have been vice president,” he added.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: 3 branches, 3 fixes: An ethics agenda for the new Congress
articles.summary: The new Congress should eschew the temptation to seek retribution against the Trump administration and instead begin the repair work needed to restore Americans’ confidence in their government.
articles.body:
This year’s midterm elections were not a mandate for vengeance — they were a demand for repair.

According to a Gallup poll released in September , 89 percent of Americans believe government corruption is widespread, a concern that topped high prices in a Fox News poll last month and tied with the economy in other major surveys. As a result, voters handed Democrats both chambers of Congress, winning even in Texas, where James Talarico became the first Democrat to win statewide since 1994 .

The new Congress should eschew the temptation to seek retribution against the Trump administration and instead begin the repair work needed to restore Americans’ confidence in their government. It should legislate ethics as three projects, one for each branch of government.

In February 2020, as chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, Sen. Richard Burr (R-N.C.) received secret briefings on the outbreak of COVID-19 . On a single day that month, he sold as much as $1.7 million in stock — long before the market collapsed — while publicly projecting calm. The Justice Department declined to charge him .

The only federal law on point remains the 2012 STOCK Act , a disclosure regime whose standard penalty for filing late is a $200 fee. Members routinely blow through that. This summer, the outgoing House passed another watered-down ban bundled with unpopular voter ID provisions, making it a poison pill designed to die in the Senate — which it will in this lame-duck session.

The new Congress should pass a clean bill restricting members and their immediate families and senior staff from trading individual stocks while in office. These should be divested into diversified funds or a blind trust. Violations should mean disgorgement of profits plus real fines. A bill would publicly call the roll and let the public see who votes to keep the trading desk open.

Next comes the judiciary. For roughly two decades, Justice Clarence Thomas accepted luxury travel from billionaire Harlan Crow , including private jet flights, superyacht cruises and stays at Crow’s private resort, disclosing none of it. Americans learned about it from ProPublica, not from the court. Under public pressure, the justices adopted a “Code of Conduct” in November 2023. But it is a code in name only.

Compliance is left to each justice. There is no way for the public or Congress to file a complaint, no one to investigate, and no consequence for a breach. Every other federal judge in the country is bound by an enforceable code. The nine most powerful judges are bound only by their own good intentions.

The new Congress should enact a binding code of ethics for the Supreme Court, with a complaint process reviewed by a panel of senior lower-court judges, mandatory written explanations for recusal decisions, and a hard cap on gifts and hospitality. Some justices insist Congress lacks the power , which is nonsense. Congress sets the size of the court, fixes the justices’ salaries and defines most of its appellate jurisdiction, and already subjects the justices to the financial disclosure requirements of the Ethics in Government Act.

Housekeeping is a legislative function. If Senate Republicans want to filibuster judicial ethics, make them do it in public.

Then comes the executive. Four months into his second term, President Trump hosted a black-tie dinner at his Virginia golf club for the 220 largest holders of $TRUMP , the meme coin he launched days before his inauguration. Buyers poured an estimated $148 million into the coin to win a seat at the table; the top 25 earned a private reception and a White House tour. Most guests remained anonymous, but 19 of the top 25 bought through foreign exchanges that are supposedly closed to Americans.

The biggest buyer was Justin Sun, a Chinese-born crypto billionaire whose securities-fraud case the Securities and Exchange Commission put on ice after Trump took office. Access to the president was, quite literally, sold on a leaderboard.

In an earlier era, that sequence alone would have produced a select committee. It still should, but the model should be documentary: methodical subpoenas aimed at money flows rather than television moments. The new Congress should follow transactions in schemes like this, then legislate to keep them from happening again. It should give the Constitution’s Emoluments Clause a statutory enforcement mechanism, end the president’s exemption from the federal conflict-of-interest statute and require divestiture or a genuine blind trust.

New legislation should prohibit senior executive officials and their immediate families from issuing, promoting or profiting from digital tokens or accepting foreign-government investment while in office, and restore the independence of the inspectors general that Trump purged in his first week back in the Oval Office. Such a move will likely draw the president’s veto to ensure the money keeps flowing into Trump family coffers. But a vetoed ethics bill can either be overridden or used as an effective campaign point for 2028.

Why start with ethics? First, to instill public confidence. Trust in the federal government is at a historic low , and nothing Democrats want to do on health care or the economy will stick if voters believe the people doing it are on the take. Ethics reform is not a distraction from the substantive legislative agenda; it is the foundation for that agenda.

Second, prevention. A stock ban, an enforceable judicial code, and a presidential conflict statute would have made each of the three scandals above either illegal or impossible.

Third, it brings the United States back into line with its democratic allies. Canadian ministers must divest or blind trust their holdings, British MPs must register their financial interests , Germany’s Constitutional Court adheres to a code of conduct adopted in 2017 . The United States spent half a century exporting anti-corruption norms, from the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act to championing the United Nations Convention Against Corruption . It is an embarrassment that in February 2025 this administration, while pursuing its own corrupt agenda, has paused enforcement of the very law we once urged the world to copy .

While many will argue that campaign finance reform is fundamentally more important of an ethics agenda item than these three fixes — and I don’t disagree — these are the areas that a new Congress can manage quickly with the American public’s mandate behind them. Any more at the outset would either be considered overreach or, in the case of campaign money, too large and complicated of a beast to tackle at this point.

Once the government is cleaned up, our new Congress can turn to unwinding tariffs, ending wars, regulating AI and rebuilding the economy. It can do the work of government, where people engage in honest disagreements the public trusts them to be disagreeing in good faith. That trust is the scarcest commodity in Washington. Restore it first. Then argue about the substance.

Michael J. Kelly teaches applied political philosophy in governance at Creighton University School of Law.

articles.title: ‘Generational change’ coming from new senators: Annie Andrews
articles.summary: South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D) has high hopes from her new Senate class and said a ‘generational change is coming.” “I said on the campaign trail we need generational change in leadership on both sides of the aisle, and what I see happening is that generational change is going to come from my freshman…
articles.body:
South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D) has high hopes from her new Senate class and said a ‘generational change is coming.”

“I said on the campaign trail we need generational change in leadership on both sides of the aisle, and what I see happening is that generational change is going to come from my freshman class,” Andrews said during an appearance on MS Now.

“We cannot revert to business as usual in Washington D.C.,” she added. “That is not what the American voters sent us there to do. We have so many problems to solve. Regardless of who the leader is, we have to get to work on day one.”

Andrews won a competitive Senate race in a historically red-leaning state against Republican Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.), who was picked to succeed her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). She won by more than 4 percentage points, according to nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ , a partner of The Hill. The forecaster narrowly favored Darline Graham ahead of the elections.

Her win in South Carolina was in line with the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterm elections where the party flipped GOP-held seats in battleground states like Texas, Kansas, Iowa and Maine, among others.

With the recent win secured by Democrat Mary Peltola in Alaska’s Senate race, the Democratic party is set to hold 56 seats in the Senate. The party also took control of the House.

The freshman Democratic Senate class includes Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, James Talarico of Texas, Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire and Troy Jackson of Maine. Some of them have said they are willing to work with the Trump administration on issues like immigration and healthcare.

Last week, El-Sayed posted mock-ups of “Trump Care” health insurance cards on the social platform X , pressing on President Trump to support universal healthcare. The Michigan Democrat wrote, “Donald this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

Talarico has also said that he wants to work with the present on issues like economic relief and immigration policy, saying that the “American people cannot wait two years for change. So we must work with President Trump.”

Much like her colleagues, Andrewshas previously said she is willing to work with President Trump “to secure the border, to stop these Medicaid cuts” and to “find a way out of this war.”

articles.title: Keep kratom opioids out of our stores
articles.summary: The easy, unrestricted access to kratom opioids should concern every American.
articles.body:
Walk into almost any gas station in America and look at the counter by the cash register. Next to the candy and beef jerky, you may find gummies, tablets and small drink bottles labeled “kratom.” Go to the refrigerated section where they sell sports drinks and you’ll see the same. The packaging is often colorful and cartoon-like. Some products come in fruit flavors. Many carry the word “natural” or “organic” on the package.

But inside many of these products is anything but natural or organic — they are concentrated, lab-made, synthetic opioids sold under the kratom name. A more accurate name for them is “kratom opioids.”

Natural kratom comes from the leaves of a tree that grows in Southeast Asia. These leaves contain chemicals that affect the brain, and people have chewed and brewed them for centuries.

But today, unscrupulous manufacturers are extracting the active ingredient from kratom leaves and chemically transforming them into far more potent substances. These products are often sold through the same retail channels that once sold dangerous synthetic drugs such as K2 and Spice — with the same tragic results.

The main kratom opioids found in gas stations are 7-OH and MGPI. Unlike kratom leaves, these lab-modified products can have powerful opioid effects that make them more addictive. The Food and Drug Administration has called 7-OH “an opioid that can be more potent than morphine,” and warns these products may be especially appealing to children and teenagers. And yet, in 15 states , there are currently no regulations for kratom opioids. Nothing stops a teenager from walking into a local neighborhood store and buying them.

So, why are leaders of United Against Fentanyl — an organization built by families who lost their teenage and adult children to fentanyl — talking about kratom?

Our most difficult challenge has never been sharing the facts about fentanyl. Although continued prevention efforts are needed, most families know that powders and pills sold by a drug dealer, or via social media, often contain fentanyl. However, many families are not aware that another opioid is today legally available to their kids at neighborhood gas stations and vape shops. These kratom opioids, dangerous on their own, can also lead to fentanyl use.

We have seen this before. A new product arrives at local retail stores. The name seems harmless — spice, K2, bath salts. They are cheap and easy to buy, and someone in a teen’s circle of friends may have already tried them. At first, there are few signs of trouble. But over time, they lead to addiction, overdose and even death.

The easy, unrestricted access to kratom opioids should concern every American. These dangerous products do not come from a street dealer or the dark web. They come from a store down the street, in a package that says it’s natural. Marketers claim “it’s just a leaf” with little to no risk.

Kratom is big business. U.S. poison control centers kratom reports increased 1,200 percent from 2015 to 2025, including 233 deaths. This report highlighted a very rapid growth in kratom exposure in 2025.

The Drug Enforcement Administration is right to act. In October, it issued a notice of intent to place concentrated 7-OH and MGPI in Schedule I, the strictest category of federal drug control. The final order could take effect as soon as this month. It is a good start, but scheduling these two substances alone will not end the threat. Congress must act.

The End Gas Station Heroin Act would ban concentrated 7-OH and MGPI, and crucially, would also cover any other synthetic or semi-synthetic opioid that is more potent than morphine. Banning a whole class of drugs based on their physiological effects, instead of an endless game of chemical whack-a-mole, helps the nation get ahead of the next threat.

The bill does not affect the sale of unaltered kratom leaf, nor does it punish people for personal possession. Rather, it targets their stronger, synthetic offshoots that are causing considerable harm to families around the country.

States do not have to wait for Congress. They should set strict age and potency limits. Store owners should take kratom opioids off their shelves. And parents should discuss the dangers of kratom opioids with their children.

The reality is that kratom opioids are harmful. They are making more people dependent on opioids. These dangerous kratom opioids must be removed from retail stores. Families suffered when we were slow to act on other dangerous drugs. Let us not make that mistake again with kratom.

Richard Baum is a former acting director of the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy and serves on the board of United Against Fentanyl. Paul Martin leads Kratom Watch and is the founder and CEO of United Against Fentanyl .

articles.title: Thune aiming for decision in next 24 hours on budget reconciliation push to fund Pentagon
articles.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is aiming to make a decision by Thursday morning on whether Republicans will move forward on a time-consuming budget reconciliation to fund the Pentagon and may make a call after the GOP’s Wednesday lunch meeting. Thune has said Republicans need to pass a budget resolution before Thanksgiving if they…
articles.body:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is aiming to make a decision by Thursday morning on whether Republicans will move forward on a time-consuming budget reconciliation to fund the Pentagon and may make a call after the GOP’s Wednesday lunch meeting.

Thune has said Republicans need to pass a budget resolution before Thanksgiving if they are to unlock the budget reconciliation process to provide an extra $350 billion to the Defense Department before Democrats take over the Senate and House in January.

“There are a few more people we need to hear from and we have some of that coming today and then we’ll have to decide whether we can proceed or not,” Thune told reporters Wednesday morning.

He said Republicans would need to take the first step toward unlocking the budget reconciliation process — passing a budget resolution — before Thanksgiving if it is to choose that route to fund the Pentagon .

“If we’re going to do it, yes, we’ve got to do it by Thanksgiving week,” Thune said after meeting with GOP colleagues over lunch Tuesday.

The budget reconciliation process would allow Republicans to avoid a Democratic filibuster, but it would require senators to slog through overnight vote-a-ramas — votes on an unlimited series of amendments — to get it done.

articles.title: The new class of Democrats won the Senate but they may struggle to find their power
articles.summary: Newly elected Democratic senators in Republican-leaning states face significant challenges in balancing party loyalty with the need to maintain diverse voter coalitions.
articles.body:
Democrats won control of the U.S. Senate, carving a path through Republican strongholds like Texas, Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina. These Democrats won in states long hostile to their party, with almost all of them offering a similar promise: independence from party leaders and cooperation across the aisle . Even still, several members of the new class are promising moderation, saying they oppose left-wing policies like Medicare for all.

Conventional political wisdom suggests that these promises of a new form of independence and moderation could make these senators some of the most powerful people in Washington. My research suggests that these senators should hit the brakes and reconsider.

The promise of centrism and the argument of their power in the Senate isn’t new; political scientists and politicos alike have long argued that centrists play a pivotal role in lawmaking and are often the proverbial kingmakers, as their vote is often the last needed to pass legislation or confirm a nominee. Others argue that polarization should strengthen the remaining moderates — as the center shrinks, their votes become essential, forcing party leaders to negotiate and giving moderates greater control over legislation.

My 2021 book, “ Life in the Middle: Marginalized Moderate Senators in the Era of Polarization ,” challenges this assumption; indeed, my findings largely contradict this expectation, suggesting that these newly elected senators have a difficult legislative path forward.

Through legislative behavior, voting records, and interviews with former senators and congressional staff, I found that moderate senators often failed to use this supposed leverage. Even still, one could argue that their influence lies behind closed doors — that because their vote is so pivotal to the passage of bills, they wield outsized influence — but my interviews with staffers and senators further suggested that no such influence exists.

Indeed, in my book, I found that on high-profile legislation that was central to their party’s agenda, moderate senators, on average, fell in line and voted with their party (think President Obama and the Affordable Care Act, for example), even if that vote was against their stated preferences. They broke from their party and demonstrated their independence when their vote was less pivotal and posed little to no risk to their party’s goals. Perhaps more revealing, moderates were also much less likely to propose amendments to help shape legislation or speak to defend or attack legislation on the Senate floor — activities that would suggest political power, or at the very least, political independence from the party brass.

All that is to say that moderates were most willing to exercise their independence when the political costs were low and relatively inconsequential. Why would senators with so much apparent leverage hesitate to use it?

The answer centers on what political scientists call traceability: the idea that voters can connect elected officials and their votes to policy decisions and their consequences. In other words, voters can see who helped produce a policy and hold that person responsible. Being visibly active in the shaping of legislation by publicly negotiating compromises makes that connection easier to draw.

For senators serving politically divided electorates, such visibility can carry serious risks.

Consider a Democrat elected in a reliably Republican state. Victory requires support beyond the Democratic base — from voters opposed to the other party and their goals (i.e. conservatives opposed to President Trump), voters drawn to the candidate personally, or those who are committed to particular policies.

Those supporters may disagree sharply about what their senator should do in office: if that senator casts the deciding vote on a controversial bill, support could alienate Republican-leaning constituents, while opposition could anger the Democratic base. Worse, compromise could disappoint both. As a result, for moderates, the question is not just which policy to support, but whether taking personal responsibility for it is worth the electoral cost. The safest course may be to keep one’s fingerprints off the legislation.

The 2026 elections set the stage for a new crop of moderates to navigate these precarious conditions. For example, in Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton — a mega-church pastor and former Republican — defeated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall to become the state’s first Democratic senator-elect in more than nine decades. During the campaign , he described himself as a “moderate or independent-minded Democrat” and pledged to work across party lines.

In Texas, James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, stressing his willingness to challenge his own party. At an October CNN town hall , he said he was running to represent Texans, not the Democratic Party, citing his bipartisan legislative record.

North Carolina’s immensely popular former governor and now Democratic Sen.-elect Roy Cooper emphasized his work with a Republican-controlled legislature, including on Medicaid expansion. During his Senate campaign, Iowa Democrat Josh Turek highlighted bipartisan accomplishments and his willingness to criticize Democrats when he thought they were wrong.

Winning in a Republican-leaning state does not necessarily make a senator moderate. According to one measure political scientists use to measure ideology , Democrat Sherrod Brown ignored the moderate playbook and had one of the most liberal voting records amongst all senators while he served in the Senate from 2007-2025.

Still, these senators share a challenge: retaining voters who agree on the need for change but disagree on what it should look like. The Democratic majority now faces pressure to advance an agenda and show it can govern, yet the senators who secured that majority in Republican states will have strong incentives to distance themselves from the party’s governing choices. Complicating things further, leaders will have to find 60 votes to overcome the legislative filibuster and navigate a hostile president’s veto threats.

For the Democrats who were successfully elected in Republican states, they will soon have to reconcile commitments to their coalition with party demands and Senate constraints. They will also learn that political power lies not with being the decisive vote, but with the willingness to own the consequences of being that decisive vote.

Neil S. Chaturvedi is director of the Weglyn Endowed Chair for Multicultural Studies and editor-in-chief of Political Research Quarterly.

articles.title: Democrats flip 9 Senate seats – most since 1958
articles.summary: Democrats have flipped nine Senate seats in this year’s midterm elections, the most since 1958, and are set to hold majority in both chambers of Congress following a sweeping victory. The last time Democrats gained nine or more Senate seats in a midterm election was during Republican President Dwight Eisenhower’s second term, the Associated Press…
articles.body:
Democrats have flipped nine Senate seats in this year’s midterm elections, the most since 1958, and are set to hold majority in both chambers of Congress following a sweeping victory.

The last time Democrats gained nine or more Senate seats in a midterm election was during Republican President Dwight Eisenhower’s second term, the Associated Press reported .

The latest win for the party came from Alaska where Democrat Mary Peltola defeated GOP incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan in a tight Senate race. The Alaska Democrat has 50.12 percent of the vote to Sullivan’s 45.79 percent, according to Decision Desk HQ .

The race was as competitive as it was controversial.

The Justice Department sued to block the results if the GOP candidate lost, arguing that an independent candidate by the same name, Dan Sullivan, would lead to voter confusion.

Last week, Mississippi showed a similar stunning result with Democrat Scott Colom defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become the next senator of the historically red-leaning state.

Before the two recent wins, Democrats were set to hold 54 Senate seats in the upcoming Congress. Now that number has risen to 56. This is the first time in 16 years that the party will hold such a large majority in the upper chamber with the last time being in 2011 with 58 seats, according to the AP report.

“56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer wrote in a post on social platform X from his campaign account. “Most people didn’t think 51 Democratic Senate seats was a possibility at the beginning of this cycle.”

Battleground states like Texas, Kansas, Maine, South Caroline and Iowa were home to the most notable Senate races where Democrats flipped GOP-held seats.

In Texas , Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in one of the most competitive Senate races in the country, turning the Lone Star State blue in a historic move. Democrat Adam Hamilton did the same in Kansas , becoming the first Democratic senator from the Sunflower State since 1939.

“With 56 seats, Democrats are in a prime position to create a durable majority that can create lasting, real results for the American people,” Schumer continued in his post.
